speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman was kind enough to give me notice of his question. As he knows, the conference on problems relating to the disabled was held in Toronto on February 1, 2 and 3 of this year, under the joint sponsorship of the departments of labour, veterans affairs, and health and welfare. At this conference varied aspects of the problems of the disabled were discussed.
All ten provincial governments were represented at the conference, along with delegates from the important voluntary agencies working in the field. As my hon. friend knows, of course the provincial governments have a principal interest in this problem, although the federal authority has certain responsibilities toward special groups, such as disabled ex-servicemen.
It may be of interest to note a fact which was brought to the attention of the conference with respect to economic maintenance now being provided for the disabled through a variety of legislative provisions. Disability

Inquiries of the Ministry pensions or allowances of one kind or another are now being provided under various governmental auspices to approximately 325,000 disabled persons. Regarding this type of problem, I am sure the hon. member will agree that it is only realistic to point out that note must be made of current international obligation and interests.
With regard to the second question, I would say that following the federal provincial conference in December of last year, and at the suggestion of the provinces, the federal government submitted to each province a draft amendment to the constitution which, if acceptable, would facilitate the realization of a contributory system of old age pensions.
Some of the provinces have agreed to the amendment in terms suggested. Others have raised questions as to its wording and effect. While the government of one province has received legislative confirmation of its authority to deal with the matter of a constitutional amendment, it has not yet indicated its final attitude.
In further replying I would simply call my hon. friend's attention to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as it is reported in Hansard for February 5, at this session.

speechtext:
I do not usually accede to my hon. friend's suggestion, but this time I think I should. The answer is as follows:
There is no standard under the Food and Drugs Act for ordinary brown bread. It has only to conform to the general requirements for bread and may or may not contain whole wheat flour, molasses, caramel or other permitted food colour without label declaration.
However, there is a standard under the Food and Drugs Act for "Vitamin B brown bread (Canada approved)". This standard 80709-46
Indian Act
provides a brown bread which is an excellent source of the B vitamins and must contain at least 60 per cent whole wheat flour- vitamin B whole wheat flour (Canada approved)-and not more than 40 per cent of a high vitamin white flour-vitamin B white flour (Canada approved). It also must contain at least four per cent of skim milk solids.
No one may advertise or mention vitamins in connection with bread that does not conform to the standard for either vitamin B brown bread (Canada approved) or vitamin B white bread (Canada approved).
The baker may choose the kind of brown bread he wishes to make, but if he sells vitamin B brown bread (Canada approved), it must conform to the standard under the Food and Drugs Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend, consolidate and clarify the Indian Act, and to provide, inter alia, for band funds and expenditures therefrom, and for other appropriations in case of deficiency, or lack of band funds.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: The minister should make a statement, I suggest.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Isn't the minister going to make a statement in connection with this matter?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
although the house is fairly well informed about Indian affairs, I shall accede to the request of the opposition and make a brief statement.
Indian legislation in Canada is almost a hundred years old. The first Indian Act was passed by the old province of Canada, in 1857, and it provided for what was then referred to as the civilization and enfranchisement of Indians. The parliament of Canada in 1869 passed its first Indian Act, which was described as an act for the gradual enfranchisement of Indians. There were two amendments between that year and 1880, at which time there was a general revision of the act.
Since that time there have been fourteen amendments, but no revision, with the result that I think all hon. members will agree with the wording of the resolution, namely that it is expedient to introduce a measure to revise the Indian Act.

Indian Act
In the years 1946, 1947 and 1948, a special joint committee of both houses of parliament met, and there was a very thorough examination of Indian affairs. The committee made a number of recommendations, both as to policy and as to practice, and suggested a number of amendments to the act. One of the most important recommendations was that there should be a revision of the Indian Act. The reason for that was obvious to all those who served on the committee. Many sections of the Indian Act had long since outlived their usefulness and by their wording were a reproach on the status which the Indian has attained in this country. In addition there were provisions urgently needed in the act to give the Indian that standard of self-determination and self-government which his status now requires.
The house will recall that last session we introduced Bill No. 267 to amend and revise the act. At that time I pointed out that if the bill were passed we would no doubt receive representations in the interval and that this session we would consider proper amendments. I hope that we shall continue to do that from year to year. The Indian Act is always subject to revision and improvement.
After the bill was withdrawn we wrote to every Indian or Indian organization, and to every white or white organization that was interested in the bill, and asked that they send written representations. The representations came in during the fall months. They have been classified and will be available to the house in due course.
In order that I might understand the viewpoints of the Indians, I visited a good many officers of the Indian organizations during the fall months, as well as a number of the larger reserves, where I consulted with their band councils. Of course I could not give any assurance as to what the legislation might be, and at the moment the Indians are as uncertain as ourselves as to what revisions there will be in the bill which will be introduced when this resolution is passed. In order to conform with what I am sure is the wish of every member of this house, that the Indians should be consulted as much as possible in connection with legislation dealing with their lives and property, we decided to invite to Ottawa representative Indians to discuss the bill after its introduction. I want to express my thanks to the leaders of the opposition parties for making that possible by agreeing that we could fix a date for the meeting, and that in all probability the resolution could be passed by that time and the bill made available. The Indians are
rMr. Harris (Grey-Bruce).]
now arriving and are prepared to discuss the bill tomorrow if it can be given first reading today.
This is an historic occasion for the Indians. Until this moment representative Indians have not sat down with a minister of the crown to discuss legislation affecting them. I hope that as a result of this conference we may have useful amendments to present to the house at later stages of this bill. I am not going to discuss the details of the bill now. It might be sufficient to say that, as the house would expect, this government has utilized the intervening time to improve this legislation, as it is doing constantly in all other respects.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear that the minister has been in touch with the Indians and other persons interested in their welfare and has received their ideas in connection with the bill introduced last year. I am glad also that the minister has asked representatives of the Indians to be here in Ottawa to discuss with him the bill which this resolution is serving to introduce. I think that is a move in the right direction. It was a course which we suggested should be followed when the bill was introduced last year. It was not done at that time, and I am glad that that mistake has been rectified.
I do not want at this time to rake over a lot of old straw in connection with the Indian question, so I shall be brief. However, there are one or two comments I should like to make. The Indian question has had a great deal of attention, both in parliament and throughout the country, particularly during the past six years. In my opinion there has been altogether too much talk and not enough action on the part of the government to remove the injustices about which the Indians have been and are still complaining.
I think the bill that was introduced last year was a regrettable mistake. In the first place, it aroused fears of all kinds among the Indians as to what was going to happen to them if the bill went through. In the second place, it destroyed high hopes which had been built up in their minds as a result of the sittings of the Indian committee, and so on, during the previous three or four years, that the new bill would constitute for them what was often referred to as an Indian Magna Carta or an Indian bill of rights. It left them in a very discouraged frame of mind, so far as I was able to see.
As the minister has said, a joint committee of this house and the other place on Indian affairs met in 1946, 1947, and 1948. That committee presented a long list of recommendations for administrative and other

Indian Act
improvements in the handling of our Indians, and it also submitted a draft bill. I am glad to see that a number of the recommendations made by that committee have been acted upon, and I think as a result the administration of the Indian affairs branch is now much improved in many respects over what it was prior to that time.
Unfortunately the bill which was introduced last year bore little resemblance in many important respects to the draft bill recommended by the committee, nor did it follow out the recommendations made by the Indians as to the kind of bill they wanted and the things that they thought were unjust and should be changed. The bill was withdrawn as a result of the strong opposition shown toward it, not only in this house but by organizations throughout the country and the Indians themselves. It was withdrawn also because of the manifest unfairness of not allowing the Indians time to study it and make representations and recommendations in connection with it. As I stated at the beginning, I am glad to see that that mistake is not being repeated this year. I am glad to learn that representatives of the Indians are here, and I presume that they will have time to study the bill and discuss it thoroughly with the minister and his officials.
I hope that the more objectionable features of Bill 267 which was introduced last year have been changed and that the changes will be approved by a majority of the Indians. There are two things in particular which I think must be changed before the bill can be acceptable, either to the Indians or to the white people who have their interests at heart. The first is the definition of Indian. The definition must be such that large numbers of Indians who have been brought up as such and know only the Indian way of life will not be thrown suddenly out into the ordinary white man's world in which they are not equipped to look after themselves or to make a living. I think one of the great objections to the bill introduced last year was the definition of Indian and the results that flowed from it. The bad effects of that definition appeared in section after section. If the new bill is to get support, that is one of the things which must be rectified.
The second point is that the arbitrary power of the minister to determine nearly everything of importance in the life of the Indian, without appeal from the minister's decision except in some cases to the governor in council, must be done away with. The Indian must be put on a par with the white man, in fact with every other citizen in Canada, so far as the right of appeal to the courts 80709-46 i
against decisions of the minister and his officials is concerned. The situation that has prevailed and that would have prevailed under the new bill introduced last year-as a matter of fact under it the situation would have been worse-was that in nearly every case decisions with respect to whether a man was an Indian, what his rights to land were under the Indian Act, and so on, were in the hands of the minister, and there was no appeal from them.
I think anything less than granting to the Indian the ordinary right of appeal to the courts against decisions of that sort makes our adherence to the United Nations declaration of human rights and fundamental freedoms nothing more than a farce. It means that in our own country we are not prepared to apply those principles to the first citizens of the land. That was perhaps the most important change that needed to be made in the bill introduced last year, and it is one which I most sincerely trust has been made in the new bill to be presented to us.
I said I would be brief; therefore I shall reserve any other comments until the bill has been presented and I have had an opportunity to study it and get the reaction of the Indians.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the introduction of this resolution, and I hope the bill to follow it will have a longer life in the house than the one introduced last year. Bill 267 was introduced last year on the 7th of June, and on the 22nd of June it was withdrawn. Like the hon. member who preceded me, I want to be brief. We cannot say very much about this matter because we do not know what is in the bill. I know what was in the bill that was introduced last year, and I am optimistic enough to expect that the new bill is going to be far better. I think the minister will have done a pretty good job on it.
It is seventy years since the first Indian Act was passed. Amendments have been made from time to time, but the grievances that the Indians have complained about so much have not been corrected. I understand from the minister's statement that he has invited to Ottawa representative Indians from the different provinces. I think that is good, and the minister must be commended for so doing. Perhaps my viewpoint is selfish, but I should like to know if he has invited a representative from the Manitoba Indian association and a representative from the unaffiliated Indians of Manitoba. He shook his head one time and not the next time, but we shall know when we see the Indians

Indian Act
who come here to represent them. I read in the newspapers that the legislature of the province of British Columbia has set up an Indian inquiry committee to deal with the welfare of the Indians. When a government will go to that extent in the interests of the Indians of their province I think they should have a representative here. However, we will find that out too.
Coming back to Manitoba, I find the greatest problem there is that the Indians still live in the past. I do not know whether that is good or bad, but when you speak to an Indian and tell him what we would like to do for him, how we are going to improve his condition, he immediately takes you back to 1871 and tells you what he was promised at that time. He tells you about the time when they met Governor Archibald and W. Simpson, the commissioner, and what he promised them.
As I see it, one great difficulty is that we gave control of our natural resources to the provinces but we never gave any protection to the Indian. We just let it go at that. When these Indians signed the treaty they were guaranteed fishing and hunting rights but they do not have those things today. There should be some compensation given to them.
I want to be brief, although I could go on for a long time because this is a subject that is close to my heart.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Go on.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I think education is the crux of the question. Indian children should be educated in the same manner as white children, so that they will look at things the same way that we do. Let us take the residential schools. Pupils are brought there from the surrounding district at the age of eight. They are kept there until they are sixteen years old, and they haive been doing everything the way that the white man does. Then we turn them loose and send them back to the reserves. They neither fit into the reserve nor anywhere else. You will find them loafing around poolrooms. I do not think we should do away with the residential schools. We will need them in outlying districts, but when we take pupils out of the residential schools we should provide vocational training to take care of them until they are twenty-one years of age. Then they will be able to take their place among the white people.
I have heard some people say that the Indian does not know anything. Do not believe that. I have travelled quite a lot among the Indians and the knowledge of some of those I have seen has really surprised me. I claim to be a first-class mechanic, having

served my apprenticeship on the river Clyde. I visited Norway House a couple of years ago, and there I saw an Indian doing something that I do not think I would have been able to do. He took two old outboard motors and made one out of them. When he told me what he was going to do I had doubts about it. The next day, however, he came put-putting down the river, and had done a wonderful job. If you go into the north country you will see Indians who are wonderful sawyers for slabbing logs and making lumber. They are as good as any white man. I have seen them do repairs that would astonish the ordinary mechanic, and they had no tools of any kind to do the job.
I always feel reluctant about praising the Liberals for doing anything.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Don't do it.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: You see the reception I get, but I want to be honest.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: So do the rest of us.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: You cannot help yourself.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: The government should be congratulated upon what it has done for the health and welfare of the Indians. When I first went among the Indians about nine or ten years ago they were dying like flies. Today the government has improved the situation.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Good old Liberal government.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
You go easy, because I could mention a great many things they have not done. Nine or ten years ago the Indian population was decreasing by about 1,000 a year. Today it is increasing by about 1,500 a year, and it can be reasonably estimated that in thirty years we shall have 200,000 Indians in this country. You cannot keep those people as wards of the government, when the country belonged to them in the first place; you must do something for them.
I do not want to take up more time, Mr. Speaker. As I said in the first place, I welcome the resolution. It will be practically impossible to please every Indian in this country, so I believe we will have to give the greatest benefit to the greatest number.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising on this occasion I am not a bit concerned about hurrying this resolution through. I believe the house as a whole has been rather remiss in its duty, on a good many occasions, in letting the resolution stage go by without much discussion, because that is the only stage during which the ordinary member has a chance of saying the things he should say without having a chairman riding him every step of the way, calling him to order and all that kind of thing. This

is the only chance hon. members have to get from the government something about what they propose to do. So let us not be too anxious about getting this thing through. Everything the government is doing for the Indians it can continue to do without a new act; and many things it is not doing for the Indians certainly could be done even without a new act. So let us take time to deliberate on this matter and see where we are going.
We may be putting through legislation which will be operative in Canada for thirty or forty years. I have had enough experience with the problems of the Indians to know that when it comes to getting reforms in respect to them, governments move dreadfully slowly, especially if they are none too keen about those reforms. So I am not promising to cut my remarks short, either at this or any other stage of the legislation, and I do not believe the minister really wants that to happen. If there are things in this act he can rectify now, I am sure he wants to do that. I have great confidence in the minister. I believe he is forwardlooking and desirous of doing the right thing as long as his influence lasts in this country, and I hope that will be for a long time, if I appraise him rightly, as I believe I do.
A minister of the crown is under a great deal of pressure, and occasionally he may yield to pressure from outside the house instead of pressure from inside. After all, this house is elected by the people of Canada to put some pressure on the government to bring about the results desired by the people, and if we exercise that pressure enough we will strengthen the hands of the ministers. So a good strong opposition does the government no harm.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to the attention of this house and of the people the fact that from 1914 to 1918 we fought the kaiser of Germany. In those days we were told, and we told each other, that we were fighting him because he dealt with a sacred treaty as a scrap of paper, when he invaded Belgium. Do you remember that? Well, Mr. Speaker, ever since 1867, when this nation was formed, Canada has been consistently and progressively breaking solemn treaties with a great people, the Indians; dealing with them not only as scraps of paper in word but in act and in fact; undermining and destroying those treaties.
We want to know whether the new Indian Act is going to make a change in this respect. Will this act see to it that we maintain with appropriate sanctity the treaties entered into one hundred and fifty years ago, which the Indians accepted at face value? It may be argued that we have no responsibility with respect to treaties made by the king with
Indian Act
the Indians back in 1763. I utterly fail to follow the reasoning of anyone who can take such a stand. Certainly when Canada took over responsibility for governing this country, she took over the responsibility that had been assumed by the king or queen of Great Britain in respect of all the people of Canada. If that is not so I fail to find reason at all in the whole situation.
What kind of people are dealt with in these treaties that we have been disregarding? The latest figures I have been able to get indicate that there were 136,407 Indians in Canada in 1949. If those were put together in one area it would make quite a respectable province. We trust their numbers will increase, because they are a great people and valuable citizens of this country. The Indians constitute a magnificent asset if only we will let them be what they want to be. If they continue to increase, as the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) indicated, before too long they may number well up toward a million. They will be good Canadians, too, far better than many of the persons we have brought here and tried to make into Canadians.
As everyone knows, the Indians -were the first Canadians and the first Americans. The Canadian Indians were never conquered; I think it well that we should bear that in mind. When the white man came to Canada the Indians welcomed him and treated him with generosity and honour; and never did they cease to do just exactly that. Whenever we had arrangements or dealings with the Indians we made treaties with them. This makes a tremendous difference in our general outlook in reference to the Indians. As I said a moment ago, the Indians of America welcomed the first white man because they had learned from their fathers that they expected the return of a great white god. That is common history, well known to every member of this house, and it is a strong indication concerning the history of the Indians. Was there a time when there was a great white god in this country? Did he set up a religion? Did he teach them right living? Did he depart, promising that he would come again? The evidence all tends to show that this was so. Therefore the Indians expected the white man and welcomed him.
Wherever the Indians of Canada yielded possession of the land and the rights they had in the land, they gave that possession under sacred and solemn treaties. These treaties, in a large and increasing measure, deprived the Indians of at least three of the much talked about four freedoms supposed to be granted by the delusive Atlantic charter. The three freedoms which, in large measure, were taken away indirectly from the Indians

Indian Act
were: freedom from want, freedom from fear and freedom of religion.
Now, by each of these treaties the Indians became wards of the Canadian government, as every member of the house and every person in Canada knows who pretends to have any information about Canada. Canada has become responsible for seeing that the Indians get adequate food, clothing, and shelter, as those constitute freedom from want. If they are to compete successfully in Canadian life, they must have education and equality before Canadian law. Without education and without equality before Canadian law, freedom from fear is simply a meaningless expression. No white man can be free from fear without a suitable education and equality before the law; how can an Indian be free from fear without those things?
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that from the day Canada took over the administration of the Indians up to this moment there has not been anything like a guarantee of adequate education or equality before the law for any *of the Indians. I realize that is a sweeping and terrible denunciation of Canada's management of the Indian problem. I do not suppose it would be well for me to discuss [DOT]this in detail just now, but perhaps I shall before I conclude this speech. The statement I have made stands capable of proof to the hilt, because Canada made treaties with the Indians as equals not on the basis of conquering them. Canada became responsible for guaranteeing the Indians security of tenure of land, and security of the right to continue as Indians.
We have done much better by our Indians in respect to those two rights. We have, in a large measure, treated the Indians' land with respect, leaving them in possession of the little bit of land we have agreed to let them have. We have also, in a large measure, guaranteed to the Indian the right to continue to be an Indian. We have done several things, however, which have made it almost impossible for the Indian to continue the religion that his father left him. We rather blithely, and in cavalier fashion, assumed that the religion we would teach the Indian was far superior in the matter of producing good men and women. I shall make no comment on the matter, but I have heard a good many Indians make rather severe comments. A good many of them have simply pointed to the effects which have been produced among them. They say no further comment is necessary.
We have, in a large measure, rendered it impossible for our Indians to retain their religion in its pure and undefiled form because, in almost all cases, we have made

it necessary for the boys and girls who wish to attain an education to attend a school directed by some religious organization whose -I almost said whose primary objective, but I will not go as far as that-objective, at least understood, was to inculcate into the boys and girls a disregard for their own native religion.
Because of the social, political and religious history of the Indians, we have assumed the responsibility of granting them a varying degree of self-government or autonomy in their tribes and bands. One of the things that are worrying the Indians wherever I have met them is this. At several places in western Canada the minister made a remark to the effect it was his intention to integrate the Indians with the white people. This word "integrate" is one of those chameleonlike words. It can mean anything you want it to mean, according to the way you use it. The Indians have every reason for fearing that it will mean there will be a deliberate ministerial and administrative pressure brought to bear on them to accept citizenship in Canada whether or not they desire it, thus becoming less and less integral parts of the tribe or band and less and less Indians. I understand the Indians do not like this very well. I maintain they have a right to dislike it and a right to resist it.
Let us look for a moment at those rights which we ought to have guaranteed to the Indians to see how far we have gone in our guarantee. First of all, what have we done in so far as food is concerned? I shall keep my eye on western Canada for the moment, because I am more familiar with western Canada. Before the treaties were signed in western Canada there were herds of buffalo roaming the plains which provided the Indians with plentiful food, clothing and even teepees. Because of policies put into operation by the government of Canada, these buffalo were destroyed, and with their destruction the source of the Indians' food, shelter and clothing was swept away. What did the government do, as a whole or as a part, to restore to the Indians a source of food, clothing and shelter following upon the destruction of the buffalo? So far as I can ascertain, not one thing.
Going a little bit further so far as shelter is concerned, when the treaties were signed- the treaty in my particular constituency was signed in 1877-there was plenty of brush; there were many trees and large areas of forest. The white man came; he cut down the trees, and in many cases he burnt them in forest fires. What was done to restore to the Indians the fuel they needed? Nothing at all. They are there today, the Blood Indians,

Indian Act
who I suppose are amongst the most fortunately situated Indians of Canada, with hardly any timber they can cut for firewood. They must buy the white man's coal, and they must give the white man the white man's dollars for the coal-and they find the obtaining of the dollars a very difficult matter.
What have we done to restore to them what we allowed to be taken away from them in the matter of fuel which is so important in the making of shelter? People will say, "Well, we could not help it." Right in that very area where these Indians are, there is coal in superabundance, and are we to be told that we could not cause that coal to be mined, and a sufficient amount of it put into the hands of the Indians, or at least rendered available to them? But we have not done anything. Does the proposed act intend to do anything? Does the bill indicate a change in policy under which the government will realize that we owe a responsibility to these Indians which we have never even attempted to discharge?
Go into the other areas and you will find a fishing problem entering in. Indians who for centuries had spent their lives fishing their food out of the streams were cut off from the streams, as happened so often in British Columbia, or found when they went to the streams that the white man had fished the fish out of the stream far down below, rendering their source of supply barren from that time on. What have we done about it? Just completely nothing. Yet in the signing of the treaties we solemnly agreed that we would allow the Indians to fish, cut trees, pick berries, hunt rabbits on the prairies and other kinds of game as long as the sun shone and the water ran and the grass grew. Sounding brass and tinkling cymbal!
These are serious matters, Mr. Speaker; they are very serious matters. The Indian has to face the problem of finding food, clothing and shelter for his children on these reserves which are denuded of all sources from which he formerly obtained these things, and we have allowed it to go on; in fact, we have abetted the white man in speeding up the denuding of the reserves or the area round about.
Let us come to education. Let us face right up to the facts. I am going to keep my eye on the Blood Indian reservation because I am familiar with it. I have had scores of the fine, noble, dignified men who constitute the elders of the Blood Indians come into my home and sit and talk to me, and ask me what on earth could be done.
There are two church schools on that reservation. I am grateful to the Roman Catholic church and the Anglican church for coming
in and establishing those schools, because they at least gave the Indians some kind of opportunity for education; but in some instances there are Indians who are living almost a hundred miles from these schools. Imagine an Indian with meagre resources setting out to take his children seventy-five miles over the prairie in order to get to one of those schools. How would we feel if we had to take our children seventy-five miles to school? The Indian now sees fine busses, fine vans, just off the reservation, going to every home practically in the countryside, picking up the boys and girls and conveying them to school every morning and back home at night in perfect comfort and ease, and in complete security through supervision, while he has nothing like that. And yet we pretend we have given the Indian a chance for education right now.
Remember, we permitted our farmers in areas probably within ten or fifteen miles to form themselves into a school district and build their little country schools to educate their children, where the distances were not too great, and where they could have the children in their homes at night; the children could help them, and they could enjoy the children. We have never done anything like that for the Indians, and apparently we do not intend to.
There has to be heart-searching; there has to be an about-face in this matter. People ask: Where are you going to get the money? Where do you think the Indians are getting the money? How do you suppose they can get the money when we, with our industrial strength and investment, cannot do it? Well, we have got to do it, if we are to be just ordinary decent people. That is all.
We cannot oblige Indians to take their children thirty and forty miles to a residential school and leave them there for weeks and weeks. We have to enable them to have schools equipped and under proper supervision and with proper teaching.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: And in contact with their parents.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
And in contact with their parents so that the children can be raised according to the will of the parents; and these parents often have pretty high ideals.
We have not begun to guarantee the Indians the education which we were in duty bound to guarantee and to provide when we signed these treaties. I think I should just read a little passage from treaty No. 7, which is the one under which the Blood Indians, along with three other tribes, surrendered almost enough territory in southern Alberta to make an empire, some of the

Indian Act
richest land to be found anywhere today, land to which we are now bringing water, and from which we are producing wealth untold. This territory was surrendered under treaty No. 7 in 1877, and I shall read to the house what is written about education in that treaty. It reads as follows:
Further, Her Majesty agrees to pay the salary of such teachers to instruct the children of said Indians as to her government of Canada may seem advisable, when the said Indians are settled on their reserves and shall desire teachers.
Of course, we know that there is an escape phrase there. There is a hole in the thing big enough for a team of horses to go through where it says: "Such teachers as to her government of Canada may seem advisable". It is clear that to her government of Canada it has not seemed advisable to supply teachers to teach these boys and girls so that they will have something like a chance to go out to school, to go into high schools and universities, to equip themselves in order that they may not have a lack of education as a handicap along with the dark colour with which God has been pleased to bless them.
We will leave education and take up equality before the Canadian law. Mr. Speaker, the ordinary Indian in Canada cannot even get before the Canadian law, much less get equality before it.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to interrupt? I do not think there is any foundation whatever for that statement.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I think before the minister is much older he will see that there is a lot of foundation for it, when everything that vitally concerns the Indian is decided by the governor in council and by agents on the reserves. And you tell me that he has a chance to get before the law? Why, a whole tribe of Indians cannot get before the law!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Oh, yes, they can.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
How far would one of us get, if he could not get before the law, if he could not go before the courts?
Let us face realities; let us do a little factual thinking.
Then I come to No. 6, security of land tenure, and No. 7, security of the right to continue as Indians. I shall not discuss No. 6 at the moment; but, with respect to the right to continue as Indians, the indications are that when the minister says he proposes to integrate the Indians with the Canadian people he could easily mean he intends to make them non-Indians. Perhaps that is not what he means, but the possibility is there. Then, with regard to No. 8, self-government, I shall say no more at the moment.

The important question that the house and country must ask the minister, if they wish to treat Indians as they ought to be treated, is this: Does the minister in his proposed new act intend guaranteeing the Indians each of the eight rights and privileges I have just set out? If he does not, then his act will be completely useless because it will fail to guarantee those rights. Now is the time for the House of Commons to find out.
After the bill comes before the house what chance have we to do anything? Every hon. member knows right well that when a bill is introduced it is immediately given first reading, at which time no one is permitted to say a word. Then, when we come to second reading we are permitted to talk about the principle of the bill. Mr. Speaker, if he is so disposed, can pretty nearly rule one out of order on almost any count, because no one can- tell us what the principle of the bill will be. Can -anyone define the principle of the Indian Act? I would like to hear several people try to do it.
After all, what good is a speech on second reading, dealing with the principle of the bill? After all hon. members have had their say, the government comes along with its steam roller and brushes everyone to one side-just as a bulldozer would sweep aside six inches of snow. Surely that is not what parliament was designed to do! Parliament was designed to be an institution which would make the government pay attention to the opposition. But the opposition has no chance in the world in the debate on second reading of a bill.
Then we come to the committee stage. There, again, the chairman can rule out of order pretty nearly anything. I have been here fifteen years and I speak with authority in the matter. I say that if we want to make any kind of effective opposition to the bill, and if we want to get anything done, now is the time to do it.
What do the Indians think of Bill 267, which the proposed bill is intended to replace? I think it was the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) who has said that we do not know what is in the new bill. Well, that is exactly the trouble. The minister may be reintroducing Bill 267 in exactly the same form, for all we know. I think we are entitled to know a little bit about how many changes have been made, and the nature of those changes. If we are not, well then v/e might as well fold up and go home, so far as this bill is concerned.
What did the Indians have to say about Bill 267? I have in my hand a document which has probably reached the desk of each member in the house. It is dated September

9, 1950, from the Caughnawaga reserve in Quebec. Everyone knows that the Caughnawaga Indians are of a pretty high type. The first paragraph of this letter states:
We, the councillors and life chiefs of Caughnawaga, St. Regis and Oka reserves duly assembled on the ninth day of September in the year of Our Lord 1950, at a grand council to discuss the merits of the proposed new Indian Act, have found that a large number of the clauses are detrimental to the best interests of the Indians.
That is a sweeping statement, is it not? Who are the people signing this letter? There are sixteen major chiefs, including Mike T. Montour, John Woodlands, Constant Albany, Joe Martin, Eddie Delaronde, John Diobo, Matthew Lazare-and there are others. Anyone who was before the committee on Indian affairs had a chance to know those splendid men. I have mentioned only some of them. Then, paragraph 2 of the letter states:
We hereby register our protest that we cannot accept the bill, as it is an entirely negative one and apparently designed to govern an inferior and subordinate people and' to keep them inferior and subordinate. It also tends to destroy the racial identity of the Indian and submerge it out of sight.
And paragraph 3:
If this bill be passed in its present form, the new Indian Act will be the most bureaucratic and dictatorial legislation ever imposed on mankind.
One might imagine that the people writing this letter are ignorant people. If they are, it is our fault: shame on us! But if they are well informed, as their letter indicates, then their words are worthy of note.
Turning to the latter part of the letter we see where these people quote history and refer to the various treaties which have been signed affecting them. We see that they are not an uneducated people. Then the fourth paragraph states:
The Hon. Mr. Walter Harris, Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, stated June 21 last that the Indian policy is the integration of the Indians. We protest against this policy of Mr. Harris, as it is our desire to remain Indians today and in the future. We are not ashamed but proud of being Indians. You would place us in the position where we would have no equality under the law but would be at the beck and call and under the control of your officials on the reserves.
And, may I add, there is no reference to the courts at all. Then, paragraph No. 5:
We Indians do not wish to become citizens of your government or any other government; we are loyal to our Indian form of government, and we want to be free to enjoy our liberty as guaranteed to us by our great constitution of the Six Nations.
There are many more things I should like to say, if I had the time. However the time now at my disposal is exhausted. I would refer to the Alberta submission. We find exactly the same thing in the submission from that province, made as the result of a
Indian Act
meeting of Indians from throughout the far-flung province of Alberta. They met in two places, at Calgary on August 17 and 18 and Hobbema on August 24. Perhaps before the debate is concluded I shall read to the house the names of the people who were there. They came, at great cost and great inconvenience, and at a time when normally the Indian is making hay and doing other things essential to his livelihood. Those men spent days giving the most careful consideration to every section and phrase in the act.
Here I have a lengthy dissertation setting forth their reactions to each section. In spite of all that careful consideration, they agree almost identically with the Caughnawaga Indians, their brethren in Quebec. I maintain that these considered, wise and careful statements from Indians condemning the act so completely cannot safely be disregarded by members of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of proceedings in connection with a bill to amend the Indian Act, as hon. members who have preceded me have said, it is not possible to discuss in detail the provisions of the legislation, for the very good reason that we have not those provisions before us. The minister has not given to the house any clear indication of the extent to which the new legislation which he proposes to introduce differs from Bill No. 267 which we had before us last year. For that reason, I think it is proper for us to make some comments on the deficiencies which we found in that legislation in the hope that they will be remedied in the proposed bill. I think it is to some extent our duty as well as our right to indicate that we object to certain provisions in the hope that an expression from the members of the house may influence the minister before the bill is actually presented and before it would be more difficult to change those provisions.
I do not believe that any hon. member of this house, however anxious he may be to become acquainted with the problems and views of the Indians, can say that he speaks as an expert, that he is qualified one hundred per cent to represent exactly what the Indians feel. But I do know that many members have made as far as they were able to an exhaustive study of the provisions of the Indian legislation, and exhaustive inquiries into the views of Indians in their own districts. One of the difficulties we find in dealing with Indian affairs is that the views of the Indians differ widely from region to region.
This brings me to the first suggestion that I wish to make to the minister on behalf of

Indian Act
the Indians of British Columbia. The Indians in the interior of the province have formed themselves into an organization known as the interior confederacy. At a meeting of that association called shortly before this session convened, and which I had the privilege of attending, the Indians considered Bill No. 267 and prepared a brief which they asked me to lay before the house and the minister.
One of the fundamental considerations in their minds was the fact that British Columbia Indians have problems quite different from those of Indians in the rest of Canada. As the minister well knows, probably the outstanding difference is that there are no treaty Indians in British Columbia. Most of the Indians in the rest of the country have their rights and positions defined by treaties which were made, either with the government or with administrators who acted before a government was formed back to the days when the country was a colony. There exists no such situation in British Columbia.
The Indians of British Columbia therefore feel that their problems and status are different. As you know, British Columbia is the one province where Indian affairs are administered by an Indian commissioner. We are unique in that particular. Our Indians feel that, their status being different, their problems being different, there should be, if not a separate act to cover the position of the British Columbia Indians, at least a separate part of the main Indian Act to deal with their situation.
I think it is fair to state or suggest as a possibility, or more than a possibility, that the difficulties of contributing to the welfare of the Indians in the rest of Canada, the difficulties of bringing them into full citizenship, are to some extent complicated by the existence of those treaties. There being no such treaties in British Columbia it is not right that our Indians should be held back and the solution of their problems retarded in any way by the fact that the solution of other problems is made more difficult or complicated by the existence of treaties. I think there is a good deal in what the Indians there have suggested and I hope the minister will give consideration to their request. I do not know whether there is a separate part or separate sections of the bill dealing with the Indians of British Columbia, but I strongly suggest that if there is not, there might well be.
I should like now to refer to a matter which has been touched upon by at least two speakers who have preceded me, the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) and

the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more). I refer to the right of appeal to the courts on the part of the Indians of this country. Surely the time has arrived when we above all other nations, having played and still playing a leading part in international and other discussions with respect to the freedom of the individual and the right of self-determination, cannot afford to perpetuate any longer a condition under which there exists in our society a class or race or nation or section of society with inferior rights in connection with the most fundamental of all freedoms, the right of free recourse to the courts.
I can see no reason, indeed I think the reverse is true, that that should be so. All that we believe when we speak of freedom and justice should not be denied to any citizen, any individual or any person in this country. .There should be granted to every one the full extent of the rights that we ourselves have had to the full, and the free right of recourse to the courts for the protection of their position; for the protection from arbitrary decisions, and the protection from injustice should be granted to 'these people. I am quite certain that if the free opinion of this house were sought every hon. member as a good Canadian would feel that the Indians must be given that right, that there is no longer any justification for denying them that right in the fullest and freest measure.
After all it is a truism, as has been said by other speakers in other years, that when it comes to a time when the survival of the country is in danger we call upon the Indian without differentiation or discrimination to join our armed forces. We all know of the wonderful contribution made by these people in the last two wars. We did not ask them to accept a lesser degree of danger or a lesser degree of responsibility or to serve in any way in a different manner from the manner in which the white soldier served.
I can see no reason why simple justice should not be granted now to these people.
I can see no reason why they should be asked when they are out of uniform to accept a lesser status with respect to that most fundamental of rights, the right of recourse to the courts. I should think that very probably no differentiation is being made now with respect to appeals for enlistment in the forces now appearing in the papers and being read everywhere we turn. I do not imagine that it is being suggested that the Indians of this country should refrain from enlisting or that they take any lesser interest in the preservation of the freedom of this nation than the rest of us. Having put that appeal before them on that basis, surely they are

entitled without further delay to having included in the bill which will follow the passage of this resolution the right of recourse to the courts.
Another matter which I submit should be dealt with adequately in the legislation to be introduced is the question of education. Not knowing the provisions of the legislation it is not possible, and probably it would not be wise at this time to attempt to discuss that in detail. Representations have been made on the subject. I have had correspondence with the minister, and I hope I can say without offence, because I know how busy he has been with this and the other matters of his department, that I am still hopeful that the matters about which I wrote him in this connection are receiving his consideration, although I am not actually certain on that point. The minister will know what I mean.
With respect to education, I feel that the legislation must preserve and underwrite the principle that no Indian shall be compelled to attend any school other than that of his denominational choice, and he should not be compelled by direct or indirect means, whether it be by direct enactment of the bill or by some agreement or understanding with any other authority in Canada. I believe that the bill should protect the right of the Indian to an education in the school of his choice.
Another matter which I think must be clarified in the legislation, because I found it was a matter of great concern to the Indians at the meeting I attended just before coming here, is the question of how far they are to give up or be in danger of losing their rights as Indians, which have been guaranteed to them, if they accept the franchise. I am by no means satisfied that the giving of rights enjoyed by white citizens need necessarily involve the depriving of the Indians of the rights which have been traditionally theirs. Their position is simply that they did not ask to be put on reserves. They are not there as a matter of their original choice. This was their country and the white settlers came. It was the white settlers who set up the reserves and, let us use plain language, confined the Indians to them. As a sop, if you like, to the conscience of the white people the Indians were told:	In return for taking your land
from you we will give you certain inalienable rights which you will enjoy as Indians on these reserves.
The Indian simply cannot see-and I think he has right on his side-why now when we say, as we should say, that we wish to give him certain rights that we enjoy, and which he hitherto has been denied, he should as a necessary part of that process lose the rights guaranteed to him when he was first
Indian Act
placed by our act on the reserve. I think the bill should clarify that point and make it clear to the Indian that in accepting these privileges of citizenship in our society he does not lose the rights and privileges which he has hitherto enjoyed.
To bring to a close this portion of my remarks, I simply wish to lay before the minister and the house certain considerations which the Indians asked me, at the meeting I have referred to, to bring here on their behalf. First, they object to any preservation of the principle whereby, as has been the case in the past, decisions of the band council on matters affecting the band where the council is entitled to take such decisions have been subject to veto of the Indian agent. That is a denial of the very system of selfgovernment, and if we wish-and I think we do sincerely-to assist the Indian to become a full citizen and to take part in all the procedures and machinery of government, then it is surely not a sound beginning on that course to say:	You cannot even have
self-government in your own band because when you take a decision it is liable to veto by the Indian agent.
They also wish to have an end of the principle that there shall be no appeal from any decision so taken by the Indian agent in that regard or decisions in other respects by the Indian agent except to the minister. I have referred previously in my remarks to my belief that they must be given the right of full and free recourse to the courts. They themselves put it that they wish to have an end of this principle of appeals from these decisions being limited to an appeal to the minister. They wish that the whole bill should incorporate the principle of self-determination with respect to their own affairs on their own reserves. The brief which they wrote and gave to me reads as follows:
1.	We unanimously oppose bill 267 in its present form and we insist that it must not be passed in parliament in Ottawa.
2.	That Indians in the province of B.C. have the handling of their own affairs so that the fears of the treaty Indians shall not be a bar to the advancement of the non-treaty Indians in British Columbia.
3.	That a better system be maintained in the promotion of agriculture, the culture of fruit, the raising and breeding of good stock by the agriculture supervisor for the Department of Indian Affairs.
Then there are two local matters with which I shall not detain the house by discussing them in detail now. We can perhaps deal with them better in committee on the bill. The brief continues:
4.	That we Indians living in the dry belt in the interior of British Columbia urgently request that our water rights be restored to us, which were given by the crown at the time of the allotment of all Indian reserves in the province of British Columbia.

Indian Act
5.	That all Indian reserve boundary lines be placed back in their original position in so far as they have been removed and some reserve land taken by whites without the knowledge or consent of the owners.
The minister has said that he has asked certain Indians to come here to consider the matter, and I sincerely hope that they will be given ample time to consider the bill before it is proceeded with further after its introduction in the house. While it is not always profitable to refer to what has happened in the past, it is fair to say that the Indians were not given a proper opportunity to consider the legislation in detail after Bill 267 was first introduced and before it was proceeded with on second reading at the 1950 session. I need only remind the minister that he appeared at first to be insistent on putting the bill through in spite of the objections that were made that the Indians had not had a fair opportunity to consider it.
For one reason or another-I think probably because of his sense of fairness which eventually came to the fore-when it was demonstrated to him that was the fact he changed his mind. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that on June 21 when the matter came up for second reading the minister took the position that second reading must be proceeded with, although we asked repeatedly that the bill be withdrawn to give an opportunity for further study. On that day at about ten minutes to eleven at night, as I recall, I moved an amendment to second reading, namely, that the bill be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence. My amendment was not designed to object specifically to any portion of the bill but merely to give some opportunity for expression of opinion that the bill should not be proceeded with simply on the ground that sufficient time had not been given for its consideration. Hansard reports that the house divided on the amendment which was negatived on division, 39 to 90. On that occasion only two members on the government side voted in support of the amendment. That night the minister indicated his intention to proceed with the bill as the first order of business the next day. Some time between eleven o'clock that night and the opening of the session the next day, however, that decision was reversed; the bill was not proceeded with, and was dropped at the end of the session of 1950.
I mention this instance, Mr. Speaker, because it shows there is a right way and a wrong way of doing things. As the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has 
said, the Indian Act is not amended so frequently that we can afford to take this amending bill lightly. The minister himself has told us that the Indian Act has been amended only some fourteen times in over fifty years, not a history of very rapid progress. Now this parliament has the opportunity to enact a real charter of rights for the Indians of this country. Parliament would not be fulfilling its responsibility either to the white people or to the Indians if it enacted a measure which did not do justice to the merits and needs of the Indians. We cannot do that justice unless we know the views of the Indians themselves. If we are sincere in our desire that they shall now embark upon a course which will qualify them for full citizenship, as I believe we are, surely one of the first steps is to ask them what they want and what they think would be the proper course to bring about that result. After all, they know themselves better than we know them. Therefore we cannot proceed with any haste between the introduction and first reading of this bill and the time it comes up for second reading.
So I ask the minister if he will give us the assurance during this debate at the resolution stage that this bill will be allowed to remain on the order paper for an adequate time before he proceeds with second reading-and I hope he will mention a minimum time-so that not only the Indians who are here may consider it, but so that hon. members may obtain the opinions and advice of the Indians in their own districts.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as yet we do not know anything about the terms of the new legislation, but we do know something about the bill which was withdrawn last year. It had plenty of room, I think, for a good many changes and improvements. Summing up the whole question of what was the matter with it, I believe the trouble is that the government treats the Indian like a child but expects him to act like an adult. In some cases, certainly along the Mackenzie, when these people were given the right to vote a couple of years ago, they had no preliminary training as far as I know in citizenship itself, only half were able to speak the English language, and only a very small fraction could write in any language.
My main purpose in rising today is to express certain ideas I have in regard to the education of Indian children. There is no difference between educating an Indian child and educating what we call a white child, except that their circumstances and environment are different and they are brought up

under different conditions. I want to add a word of commendation to the minister on the improvement of those conditions over the last number of years.
I hold several ideas, which I think are held by the Indians themselves. The first is that the Indians want to see education divorced from the churches. Let me make myself perfectly clear. I admit immediately that the churches have done marvellous work, particularly in the north, and that without that pioneer work the northern Indians would be largely pagan and unlettered. But just as the time arrived in our own system of education when the greater part of the functions had to be taken over from the churches by the state, so I think the time has now arrived when we should introduce into our system of Indian education the same type of public schools we ourselves have. In pioneer days not only education but medicine and many other things were part of the work of the missionaries. The Indian, I think, feels the time has come for the government to take over a good many of those functions which the missionary was asked to perform but which I do not think are in the sphere of the church.
Here I want to pay tribute to the work of the residential schools; but in many parts of the country the Indians are asking for public schools, and that those schools be in their own settlement. I think there is a valid argument for that point of view. Many Indian children living at home are being given no schooling at all. The education of Indian children in the Northwest Territories is directly the business of this parliament, so this is one debate on education when this matter of provincial autonomy, which shows itself in every discussion of the kind in this house, will not be dragged in. In those territories this government is responsible; both the government public schools and the denominational day schools are maintained directly from the exchequer of this country.
In the early days any education obtained by the Indians, and indeed by the white people, was acquired at the mission. The teaching was done voluntarily, as an act of charity. Later small grants were given by the government and books and certain simple equipment were provided. In recent years I believe the government has been paying practically all the costs of these mission day schools, except the cost of the buildings themselves and their maintenance. Now there is a demand for public schools. If what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) says is correct-and I am not saying whether or not it is-and the primary object of the
Indian Act
church sponsors is not always simply education in the ordinary sense, then the government is subsidizing denominationalism at least to some extent.
The problem is how education may be best brought to the Indian child. I believe it should be brought to him and not that he should be brought to it. How are we best to introduce the world to these children in the development of their bodies, their minds and their intellects through the media of science, literature, history and such handwork as we think may be best adapted for them? The development of skills and handwork, I believe, should be an important part of the education of these people, who are accustomed to use their hands and who are used to living in the open spaces. Such an education would aid Indian children in their enjoyment of life, and their ability to be independent in earning a living.
I have said that, when introduced to our civilization, the Indian young people seemed to pick out the worst things. Someone has talked about the young men hanging around the poolrooms and such places. It would seem to me that our task would be to give them a taste for the first-rate things. There is no way that can be acquired unless they are somehow or other brought into contact with those things. At this point I should like to offer some general principles, ideas or suggestions.
I believe that statistics show, although I have not the statistics with me, an increase in the number of day schools. I am in favour of this. One great advantage of the day school to my mind is that the child is in touch with his parents and his home, at the same time as he is with education. I think my argument is sound when I say that the child, being educated at a day school and going home nightly, has as much effect upon the parents and the home as the educational institution has upon the child himself. In that regard I believe the day school is far superior to the residential school. The danger of the residential school is that the child is taken seventy-five or a hundred miles, whatever the distance may be, away from his home and, for the time being, seems to enter a foreign country in which things are altogether different. He does not see the application of those ways to his own way of life or to the manner in which his parents earn their livelihood. He is in that foreign land until he leaves it to return to the land of his birth. Then, he simply throws up the whole thing and says there is no use in trying to adapt new ways to the old mode of life. He again becomes immersed in the habits in which he was brought up from early childhood.

Indian Act
May I say that habits of health and sanitation are two of the things that come immediately to my mind in that regard. On the other hand, if a child is going back and forth to his own home while he is in contact with these other rules of health and other methods of sanitation, he becomes a missionary for those better ways of life.
The attendance of Indian children at school should commence at the same age as the attendance of white children, if the schools are available to them. I believe I know something about the psychology of teaching young people, and to my mind one of the greatest tragedies I see in the residential schools throughout the country is to find a boy at an advanced chronological age doing the simple work of the primary grades. It is something in which they have no interest. I say it is a tragedy, and I mean just that. The Indian children will have to start school at the same age as we start our own children, at the stage where the chronological age, may I say, fits ,he social surroundings. I believe that my neaning at least is clear, even if the term is rot perhaps the most suitable. We have that sort of tragedy in schools other than Indian schools but it is found often in Indian schools, because when these children have to be sent away from home the parents are not willing to allow them to go until they are past the age at which we send our children to school.
The system of education, whatever it is, of Indian children has not been too successful in the past, even if I have granted that it is on the mend. This is a sad reflection on our education of the Indians. In 1945 only 71 Indian children were registered in Grade IX. It is true that there were 219 in 1949, and that is an improvement, but that is very few for the whole of Canada. I am speaking now, of course, of high school education. In that same year, 1949, only 65 children were enrolled in the three grades X, XI and XII. I have no figures as to whether they were successful in those courses, but at least they were enrolled in them.
The residential schools, in which most of these people in high school grades were enrolled, are not as efficient as they might be. The main reason for this is lack of funds. Too many children, for example, who are attending these schools are paying for their education, in many cases in the form of work. I have no fault to find with work. Work is a part of a person's education; I believe those children should be allowed to work, but- note this-only when that work is a part of the educational process. Where you have children in a boarding school away from their parents and there is a lot of work to be done around. the school farm, there is room for abuse. The temptation is to allow those

children to get on with the job of making the place nice, cultivating the garden and so on, so that when the inspector comes everything will look well. As I say, there is room for abuse in that system.
Another thing I have noticed about the Indian schools is the lack of playground equipment. These Indian children take naturally to sports, and sports could be used as a medium for their instruction, for moral uplift and for inculcating in them a sense of fair play and honesty. It could be used to teach them to be modest winners and good losers. For some of these ideas which I have expressed, I am indebted to Dr. S. R. Laycock, who is a prominent educationist and psychologist in my own province. He is nationally known, indeed internationally. In 1950 he was chairman of the school and education committee of the Canadian home and school and parent-teacher federation. This organization presented a brief, I believe to this government but at least to the minister, over Dr. Laycock's signature. The brief was dated November, 1950, and recommends many valuable things. I should like to conclude my speech by putting those recommendations on the record of this house where they may be available for all the members to study. The recommendations are as follows:
1.	That the federal government increase the funds available for the building of schools among the Indian people and the proper conduct and maintenance of these schools. This is in accordance with the recommendation of the former director of Indian affairs. Mr. Hoey, who, we understand, recommended to the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons that a minimum sum of twenty-five millions annually for twenty to twenty-five years would be necessary to rehabilitate the Indian.
2.	That whereas it requires $300 a year adequately to feed and house a child in a residential school, and whereas Indian children are entitled to as good care as other children in Canada, the federal government increase the annual per capita grant to all residential schools for Indian children to at least $300 per child and exercise such supervision as will ensure that the total grant so made is used for its intended purpose.
3.	That provision be made to provide adequate facilities for manual arts and home economics in the Indian day schools.
4.	That adequate playground equipment be provided for all Indian schools.
5.	That the Indian Affairs Department instruct its branch in each province to obtain from the provincial federations of home and school or parent-teacher associations, literature concerning the aims of home and school or parent-teacher associations and to forward copies to interested parents of children in Indian schools and that all authorities of the Indian Affairs branch be instructed to encourage the formation of home and school associations in Indian schools.
I submit these recommendations, Mr. Speaker, to the consideration of the minister and of the hon. members and of the government.

speechtext:
I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on taking early action in this session to bring down this important legislation. I may say it is somewhat disappointing to many of us that it was not possible to proceed with the bill introduced at the last session, but no doubt the delay will prove helpful, in that it has provided wide opportunity to the Indians themselves to make further representations, and to others interested in the subject to submit their views on what might be done by legislation to improve the lot of our Indian people.
It was in 1946 that the parliamentary committee, composed of some thirty-two members of the House of Commons and of the other place, was set up to study the existing Indian Act. This committee laboured for three years, during which representative Indians from across Canada, and representatives of religious denominations and other groups interested in Indian administration, were called to give evidence.
The various parties of the house were well represented on this committee. I should say that those of us who have perused the reports of the proceedings of the committee could not help but be impressed with the magnitude of the task performed, and the sincere and painstaking efforts taken to meet, to the fullest possible extent, the responsibility placed on its members to set up the framework of a new and better Indian Act.
There are, in the riding I have the honour to represent, over 5,000 Indians, and like my colleagues from the Cariboo and Skeena I am greatly interested in the proposed bill.
It is not likely of course that this measure will find favour in the eyes of all the Indians of Canada, nor yet be satisfactory in every way to all those interested in Indian affairs. No legislation of such scope and magnitude ever does. I should say, however, that to me it does represent a sincere and honest effort on the part of government to improve the Indian Act.
There has been a great deal of criticism of the Indian Act, and to some considerable extent, by those who probably never took the time to familiarize themselves with what it contains. In this regard it is interesting to note that there are important groups across Canada who are quite satisfied with the existing Indian Act and do not wish any revisions of any kind made to it; while others will be content with some minor changes.
The proposed measure is no doubt designed to give wider power to the Indian people in the management of their own affairs. It is noted with satisfaction that representations
have been made to have this extend to a greater control of their band funds, the sale of produce and stock, and lease and sale of reserve lands. This would be all to the good. Some of the very objectionable features of the existing statute should be dropped.
I refer particularly to the provision against the collection of band funds to prosecute Indian claims, and to the provision to expropriate Indain lands adjoining a municipality in excess of 8,000 population. No such laws hold against any other racial group in Canada and, consequently, could be held to be of a discriminatory character.
The passage of the proposed legislation, however, will not provide all that is required to improve the lot of the Indian people; for without adequate funds to continue and extend the very commendable program of school construction, housing and other worthwhile projects commenced a few years ago by the Indian department, the new bill will fall far short of what it is intended to accomplish. I will, therefore, be interested to see what provision has been made in the forthcoming estimates to continue these very necessary undertakings.
Surely, when it is possible for this country to extend generous assistance to the underprivileged people of other lands-I am thinking of the Colombo plan, and I have no objection to it whatever-we should be prepared to meet, without hesitation, the needs within our own gates of a people whose roots are very deep in this land of ours, and to whom we have a very heavy responsibility.
There should be no unnecessary restrictions on the school and welfare programs of the Indian department, for there could be no justification for such a move, short of war itself, and especially when one recalls the niggardly treatment of this department in the matter of the provision of funds prior to 1944, which a perusal of the estimates prior to that year discloses.
