I came within a year,
anyway. As I said at the outset, I am deeply interested in the Indian people of Canada, and particularly those resident in my own riding, which contains the Yukon Territory and the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories. It is my responsibility, as a member of this house, to be so interested. I intend to continue to press for those services which are necessary to improve their lot.
The condition of our native population in this area is not a happy one by any means. These people need our sympathetic help to become good and self-reliant Canadians, and much remains to be done. In the northern

Indian Act
areas the widest possible freedom should be given to the Indians in the matter of taking fish and game for food purposes. The Indian is a conservationist by nature, and he will not kill unless necessity demands.
It has been necessary for the Indian people to adapt themselves to the impact of this civilization. In the older parts of Canada this process of adaptation is proceeding successfully and I for one am happy to say that their health and economic situation is improving- perhaps not as much as we would like, but still the tide seems to have turned and the trend is upward.
I am not unmindful of the devoted efforts of the missionaries and public servants in the north; of the splendid work of the doctors and nurses of the Indian health services under the able direction of Dr. Percy Moore, and officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the sympathetic understanding of their many problems by director D. M. MacKay and his efficient and loyal staff.
Much has been done, especially since the second world war, in improving the health of the natives in the north. The establishment of the Charles Camsell hospital at Edmonton gives hope that that dread disease, tuberculosis, may be banished entirely. With the campaign to improve health conditions should go a campaign to improve housing, living conditions and hygiene. Much has also been done in improving educational facilities for the natives in the past few years, and I am mindful of the many fine schools which have been opened in the north in recent years.
These schools should not confine their teaching to the three R's. They should teach trades so that the Indian people can take their rightful place in building the many houses and buildings that will be required; in the greatly expanded mining industry and in operating tractors and machinery used in maintaining and constructing roads, highways, hydro developments and other engineering works and projects that are already built or will be constructed.
In my opinion every endeavour should be made to create employment for them. Many of them are natural-born mechanics and are proud of their already acquired skills. We must not only give them every opportunity to learn these trades but we must give them encouragement and opportunities for employment.
While thinking of the welfare of those natives who should and will take part in the development of our great northland, we should not overlook the welfare of those who for many years to come will continue to depend upon hunting and trapping for a

living. They should be encouraged to husband and develop their resources of game and fur-bearing animals in the same way that a wise farmer tills his farm or a wise rancher develops his herds.
Something should be worked out to afford the native trapper a measure of economic stability and stable prices for his furs, as is given to the farmer for his products, as it is a recognized fact that their economic conditions depend to a large extent upon the fluctuations of the fur market-and this means either hunger or plenty for the native trappers of northern Canada.
Another matter of concern to the native population of my riding is the fact that carpenters and labourers are brought in to the Mackenzie river districts from Edmonton and other large centres by government departments, at great expense, to work on the various projects, when there are already many residents who have the skills and ability and willingness to do the job in hand, and who can do it equally well, if not better, and at much less expense. I trust the departments concerned will discourage this practice and make provision for the employment of local people on northern projects.
I commenced by congratulating the minister upon bringing in this legislation at the present time. I conclude what I have to say by congratulating him again upon the evidence we have had of his keen and kindly interest in the Indians of Canada which, indeed, augurs well for their administration under his guidance.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this resolution I shall not attempt to emulate the eloquence of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) in either the length or the quality of my remarks. I propose chiefly to refer to the matter of education as it affects the Indians.
Before doing so however I would preface my remarks by stating that we have not many Indians in Newfoundland. I believe they number less than a thousand in all, and that they are situated chiefly in the ridings of Grand Falls-White Bay and Burin-Burgeo. The original inhabitants of the country, the Beothuks, have now been completely killed off by the original white settlers. The few tribes remaining are the Montagnais and the Micmacs. I believe they came from the mainland.
In this connection I should like to bring to the attention of the minister an article which appeared in our local press in Newfoundland when this matter was under discussion last year. This article from the

Evening Telegram of St John's is dated at Ottawa, March 25, and states:
Newfoundland will continue to take care of the Labrador Indians and Eskimos, but will do so at federal expense, for education, relief and social services, it was reported here today.
Representatives of the Labrador area, Messrs. T. G. W. Ashbourne-
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay.
-and Mr. Horwood-
The provincial member for Labrador.
-have been trying to have the federal government take over the care of the Labrador natives for some months now. Failing that, they have asked for a per capita grant to the provincial government to take care of the Indians and Eskimos.
The present arrangement has been made, it is understood, because there are so few natives in Labrador that the federal Indian affairs branch didn't feel justified in setting up special administration facilities to take care of them.
Just how Newfoundland will be compensated for the care of education, relief and social services for the Labradorians is presently unknown, but it is felt that some scheme like Messrs. Ashbourne and Horwood's per capita grant will have to be worked out.
According to a Canadian Press message from Ottawa the government has decided against "the retrograde step" of putting the Indians of Newfoundland on the same restricted citizenship basis as the other Indians of Canada by bringing them under federal legislation.
That means, a Senate committee was told today, that the newest province continues to be the only one in which the Indians-200 to 300 members of the Micmac tribe-have the same citizenship status and privileges as the white man.
The information came from D. M. MacKay, head of the Indian affairs branch of the new Department of Citizenship and Immigration and one of a number of departmental officials to testify before a committee studying their estimates.
Mr. MacKay's evidence about the Indians of Newfoundland brought congratulations for that province from Senator Reid. He thought it was a good thing.
Senator Cairine Wilson (L-Ontario), chairman, said full citizenship for Indians is the objective set for all Canada by Prime Minister St. Laurent.
Mr. MacKay said it was hoped Newfoundland provides another example in Indian life.
In connection with this same matter I should like to quote an article which appeared in the Guardian of April 1, 1950. I am not sure where this newspaper is published, but I believe it is published in Charlottetown, in the constituency of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure). This reads:
The education of Indians in Labrador is being left in the hands of the Newfoundland government with the federal government footing the bills as well as those for relief and social services. Colonel D. M. MacKay, director of the Indian affairs branch, has explained to a Senate committee that Indians in Newfoundland have the same citizenship status and privileges as white Canadians, and that the government does not propose the "retrograde step'' of bringing them under paternal federal legislation. The decision is a wise and just one, as is the proposal to grant full citizenship rights to Indians in
Indian Act
the other provinces. The existing situation is certainly not one of which this country can be proud. That the descendants of original inhabitants should be treated as being children all their lives shows small regard for their capacity to run their own lives and operates to make it almost impossible for these people to develop their natural abilities. It would seem, according to Colonel MacKay's statements, that the position is worse in the mari-times than the other provinces. At least in the rest of the country it is not the policy of the government to segregate the children in the schools. How such a policy came to be adopted in the maritimes is not very clear, but the sooner it is reversed the better. Probably no better solution could be found for this particular problem than assimilating the younger generation into the general provincial school system although it is a federal obligation to provide ways and means.
I hope that the arrangement with Newfoundland, referred to in both these articles and the one in which the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay (Mr. Ashbourne) has taken such an interest, will be continued in Newfoundland in the future. It has worked very satisfactorily. I understand that the federal government provides the money and the provincial government undertakes to look after the services for the Indians and Eskimos. Certainly, in so far as the educational system of the province is concerned, it meets fully the requirements of the terms of union.
As I said at the start, I am going to be brief and on the general resolution I shall confine my remarks to a few words with respect to education. I want to associate myself with the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) in what he has said on this subject and to say quite definitely that in my opinion there should be written into the new bill, if it is not already there, a guarantee that there will be freedom for each denomination in its endeavours toward spiritual achievements, and freedom of conscience of the individual for whom religious instructions are intended.
I understand that under the present act these questions are taken care of by ensuring that the schools shall be denominational in character and with the further stipulation that the Indian child shall receive education in the institution of his religious belief. I understand that the previous act provides for the creation of schools having religious characteristics similar to those of the children attending the school. I submit that the proposed bill should guarantee the right to establish denominational schools.
I believe that the minister received the latter part of last year a brief from the Canadian Catholic conference on this subject and I hope he has given this matter proper consideration in the drafting of the proposed bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members are

Indian Act
anxious to do what is best for the material and social welfare of the Indians, and I believe they are also interested in the intellectual welfare of the Indians, but so far no one has spoken in support of the spiritual welfare of the Indians. I have heard some criticism of the manner in which that has been carried out. I had not intended to speak until I heard the astonishing remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) to the effect that the Indians wish to have education divorced from the church. I question that. For whom was he speaking? Has he taken a plebiscite of the Indians across Canada to find out if that is their sentiment, or is he speaking for only a small group?
If we look over the history of this country 1 think we will find that the Indians owe a great debt of gratitude to the missionaries right from the early days when Champlain came here-the missionaries were here before him-the days of the Franciscans who left this country to go to southern California. In that part of the continent they found the lowest grade of Indians on the face of the earth and trained them in the arts of civilization and built up those wonderful missions known as the jewels of the rosary of Junipero Serra and which stretch from San Diego to San Francisco up along the California coast.
Anyone who is familiar with the duties of missionaries knows of their self-sacrifice, their devotion, and the hardships that they suffer from the moment they enter upon their missions; the loneliness they have to put up with, and the long distances they have to travel, and they certainly will recognize the debt of gratitude that the Indians owe to these self-sacrificing and devoted missionaries.
The Franciscans left Canada to go to southern California while the Jesuits left southern California to come to Canada. It seemed to be a good exchange. The first Jesuit missionaries to come to Canada included those remarkable men who, by their long-suffering, their patience, their perseverance, their devotion and finally their martyrdom, showed that they were ready to do a great service for all who came after them as well as for the Indians whom they served. For eight years they lived amongst the Indians in Huronia without making a single convert, and always with the fear of a hatchet landing on their heads and taking their lives. One of them, Father Isaac Jogues, after suffering great cruelties, escaped to France to come back again and suffer martyrdom at the hands of the Iroquois across lake Ontario. It seems to me that the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has spoken without thinking of the historical aspect and of the great contribution which missionaries from those (Mr. Browne (St. John's West).)
early days up to the present time have made to the lives of the Indians of Canada. He states that the missionaries used to teach and give a little medical service. That is certainly the most inadequate and unjust summary of the duties of a missionary that I have ever heard. He said they should be replaced by public schools, that a time came for all of us when teaching by missionaries, i.e., by religious, was done away with and replaced by public schools.
I do not agree with that statement. I contest it. What is the purpose of education? Is it to make man possess a lot of knowledge of facts that he can get out of encyclopaedias? Is he to forget the true purpose of life? Missionaries are concerned with that aspect. They are concerned with more than the material or even intellectual advancement of their charges. They are concerned with the spiritual and moral purpose of life, and we should all be concerned with that. Although some people may honestly feel that the public school system of education is better, I think it will be found in the long run that the system of education that stresses the spiritual side of life is preferable.

It is not the
Indian adults who go to school; it is the Indian children. That raises a question which I do not propose to enter into at the present moment. I know little of the modern conditions existing among the Indians of this country. I have not seen many of them for a long time. I remember the Indian reservation at Fort William and the one north of Peterborough. I recall the reputation they had at that time, and what I saw at Fort William showed that the government was certainly neglecting them.
The hon. member also made a statement- and it only has to do with Indians indirectly- that education was not in the sphere of the church. That is the chief function of the church. That is the very reason for its existence-to teach people the proper way to live. Why did God make man, and so forth? We must not forget such things. When we open our daily sessions we say prayers, and yet we want to divorce religious training from the education of the Indians.
As I have said, by their self-sacrifice, devotion, courage and perseverance the missionaries have shown that they are the best

friends the Indians have. Sitting in our comfortable quarters we are apt to forget the terrible hardships and anguish that missionaries have to undergo, not only in the more prosperous places such as southern Alberta but also in northern Labrador and the Yukon, places where the Indians are sometimes scattered over hundreds of miles. The missionary who goes amongst them has many problems, the duties of finding schools and teachers, building churches, and teaching religion as well as the problem of transport, and, sometimes, the problem of getting in touch with the member of parliament and the department in order to get things done.
The Indians have shown that they could survive persecution by those who were not missionaries, by the same type of man from whom public school teachers have been drawn, by laymen. They have survived persecution, enslavement, massacre, despoilment and neglect. I believe in the past five or six years more progress has been made in the methods of teaching than had been made for a long time before. I had the privilege of speaking to one of the teachers in an Indian school recently, and at the time I went as fully as I could into the matter. He told me that Indian boys and girls are just as bright as white boys and girls, and that they have done wonderful things in sports. They are better athletes than white children. I am referring particularly to the school at Spanish where there are 175 boys. I believe that is on Georgian bay. The boys and the teachers have built the school. It is a splendid structure. They spend a certain time studying and a certain time at manual labour.
The hon. member for Saskatoon said that a few years ago there were only about ninety in grade IX throughout the whole of Canada. Here there are 175 in one school, and there are two schools at Spanish. This year I believe there were twelve who matriculated in grade XII, and some of them went on to Loyola university at Montreal. I believe it is a very successful project. I was surprised to find that the missionaries receive no salaries. They are teaching there and are not receiving any salaries. I believe if the government will maintain the same interest that the minister now seems to be showing in the Indians, and will conduct research into the Indian problem, the Indians will advance, become happier and more prosperous, and the people of Canada will have reason to be proud of the manner in which they treat the Indians.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the business of the house of course is not confined to the Indian bill. We hope that the session will not last too long before we prorogue, and it may be necessary to take the bill at any time and deal with it. The Indians who are here will be considering the bill until the end of this week. If they are able to reach a conclusion about it by that time it may be that some of the points my hon. friend has mentioned will be cleared up in his mind. the second reading of Bill No. 75, to incorporate Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited.

May we have an explanation
from the sponsor?

The powers requested in the
bill, the second reading of which I am now moving, are similar to the powers granted in other bills which have been passed in this house.
Under this bill incorporation is being sought for a gas pipe line company under the Pipe Lines Act, being chapter 20 of the 1949 statutes of Canada.
The bill of course follows the usual standard form of pipe line bills under this act. The purpose of the act is as follows: In view of the tremendous developments of the gas and oil industry in Alberta, certain principles were laid down by the act under which people who were desirous of having an interprovincial or international pipe line constructed would have to come.
As hon. members well know, under the Pipe Lines Act jurisdiction rests with the board of transport commissioners, and although the passing of this bill does not in any way establish a route which this proposed pipe line will follow, as that is within the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners, yet I have been authorized to say that the very purpose of this proposed company is to build a gas pipe line from Alberta to Montreal, following an all-Canadian route, and paralleling the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway and of the

Canadian National railway. It will be approximately 2,200 miles long with collecting lines and lateral lines of 900 miles. In view of the type of debates we had on pipe line bills not so very long ago concerning an all-Canadian route I venture to say that some people got certain ideas and that may be the reason why this bill is before this house today.
' The communities that are to be served are as follows: in Saskatchewan, cities and towns along or within reach of the Canadian Pacific railway main line, including Swift Current, Moose Jaw and Regina; in Manitoba, cities and towns along or within reach of the Canadian Pacific railway main line, including Brandon, Souris, Portage la Prairie, Winnipeg and St. Boniface; in Ontario, towns and industries from Kenora to Sudbury, including Fort William and Port Arthur, Steep Rock iron mines and paper mills at Red Rock, Terrace, and Marathon. From Sudbury the line will go south to Toronto, with spur lines west to London, Galt and Kitchener, and on to the depleted gas and oil fields of western Ontario where gas will be pumped into underground storage in summer months. From Toronto the line will go east following the Canadian National railway lakeshore line and serving Oshawa, Kingston, Port Colborne, Brockville, Prescott and Cornwall, with a spur line up to Smiths Falls, Ottawa and Hull. In Quebec, it is proposed to serve the communities along the Canadian National railway route from Coteau Junction to greater Montreal. Ultimately it is hoped, with the increased capacity of the line, to extend it along the north shore of the St Lawrence as far as Quebec city.
There is of course another federal act which exercises control, namely, the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. However, it is my opinion that this act would have no application, because all consumers will be in Canada and no gas will be exported out of Canada.
The mere fact that this bill should go through does not mean that any gas will be taken out of Alberta without the consent of the provincial government. In 1948 the provincial government of Alberta passed an important act dealing with gas known as an act to provide for the preservation, conservation and effective utilization of the gas resources of Alberta. I am not going to go into the details of this act. I believe that after the bill receives second reading hon. members will have an opportunity to go into it further in the appropriate standing committee.
Alberta's stand, as hon. members are probably aware, is that no natural gas will be taken outside of that province unless the
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines requirements of Alberta have been assured first. Since I come from Alberta, may I say that in that province we are concerned with the development of the gas and oil industry in Alberta. The attitude that the provincial government takes in this matter may be stated in the recent report of the Alberta conservation board and certain recommendations which it makes. These recommendations were made only a few weeks ago. The stand of the premier of the province can be seen in the publication called "Within our Borders", dated February 15, 1951. Although this publication is not official, I think the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) will agree with me that it is almost semiofficial. This is what the premier of the province says:
The government is satisfied that the board has made a thorough and comprehensive investigation into the matter of Alberta's gas reserves and the provincial requirements and concurs in its conclusions and recommendations.
The board finds that Alberta's present established gas reserves are approximately equal to the amount of gas the board estimates is necessary to ensure that the present and future requirements of the province and accordingly recommends that these reserves should be further increased before the export of gas is approved.
The government concurs fully in the board's further conclusion that as quickly as additional reserves are established it will be in the best interests of the people of Alberta to make surplus gas available for sale outside the province in that an export market will:
(a)	Encourage and speed up the development of our petroleum and natural gas reserves.
(b)	Encourage and make possible greater and more rapid industrial development within Alberta.
(c)	Make gas available to Alberta communities which otherwise could not be served.
Then the premier's statement goes on in this way:
It is evident that by carrying out the recommendations of the board's interim report the requirements and interests of the people of Alberta will be fully protected while at the same time we should experience an accelerated exploration and drilling program for natural gas which should result in a surplus of gas for sale outside the province.
Then the premier goes on to say that to facilitate this development the government is amending its gas exploration and leasing regulations along the lines recommended by the board to encourage the more speedy development of our vast gas resources.
In any event this shows the stand taken by Alberta. I suppose we may expect that some other groups will seek incorporation. I hope there will be more people who will do so. We in Alberta would like to find ourselves in a position where there will be competing companies endeavouring to get our surplus gas reserves.
May I point out further that the main transmission line of this proposed company, from

Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Alberta to Toronto, will be a thirty-inch pipe, and from Toronto to Montreal a twenty-four-inch pipe. It is estimated that the cost of this line will be about $250 million. The passing of the bill has important national considerations. To begin with, it is an allCanadian route and, with the total volume of gas consumed in Canada, complete control will be ensured in this country. Secondly, it will make possible the replacement of foreign coal and oil for fuel purposes, thus saving many American dollars each year. Third, it will certainly be of great benefit to Canadian industries along the route.
Since Alberta is emerging as one of the world's great storehouses of gas, which is a valuable fuel and source of quick energy, the aim of this pipe line is to make the exportable surplus of the Alberta gas available to central and eastern Canada, in accordance with the recommendations made by the Dinning commission, and of course also in accordance with the policy of the people of Alberta, to dedicate the wealth of gas in that province first to the needs of the people of the province, secondly to the needs of Canada and, thirdly, for export purposes.
Many of the facts in connection with this proposed company, which I did not mention and some of which I do not even know, could be brought out after second reading, when the bill is referred to the appropriate standing committee.

Mr. Speaker, I support the bill for some very clear reasons. In the first place it is not going through the Fraser valley, Vancouver or the United States. It is an all-Canadian route. Usually those who are putting up the money to pay for a pipe line, or for anything else, have some say in the matter. We are convinced now, by those who are putting up the money, that this will be an all-Canadian route, that it will come from Alberta, and that it will come to Fort William, the hub of Canada. Then it will proceed to Port Arthur, and from there to Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto.
I intend to make only a short speech, because we want this bill to go through in short order. It is a gas bill, but we do not want any more long speeches than are absolutely necessary. We would appreciate criticism, but we believe that this is an opportunity for Canada to have an all-Canadian route, and we will support it.
This company deserves credit. It was pointed out the other day that there was not sufficient gas to encourage these people to go ahead. Well, we see what happened. This company with its engineers went ahead and


discovered seven additional sources of gas- not just one. So there is all kinds of gas to keep this pipe line going.
There is something further involved in connection with the pipe line. It is to follow a railway line, and will not need to be buried deep in the ground. It will require to be buried only 12 or 15 inches, perhaps less, for protection from wild animals or from those people who might want to get a little gas cheaply. Frost will not disturb the gas in the line; in fact it will be an aid to it.
We had a good deal of difficulty when we failed to get the oil pipe line to the lakehead. While at that time the people who were putting up the money had a good deal of say in the matter, they did not have more say than some of the people in the House of Commons who did not know as much about it. This time we are taking no chances. We are going to do our best to have this pipe line allCanadian, and have it go through the lake-head to serve the whole nation.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a great
pleasure this evening to witness the conversion of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). Just a few short months ago he was doing his best to prevent us getting a Canada-first gas pipe line through British Columbia. Now however he seems to be sold on the policy of Canada first, and I am very grateful that he has come over to our side, even at this late date. It shows that there is always hope. I would hope, too, that many of his fellow members, who saw as he did last year, will also have seen the light in the intervening months.
I thought this evening that the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) made a very frank and full statement about the routing of the pipe line. That is the kind of information to which members of the House of Commons are entitled, in respect of all these bills seeking to incorporate pipe line companies.
In view of the fact that the pipe line is to serve Canada first, and in fact in this case it will serve Canada only, I for one am very glad to support it. I believe it would be most unfortunate if any effort were made to talk out the bill and, unless in the standing committee we find something unsatisfactory, I shall certainly support it.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the house and I rise merely to congratulate the hon. member on the excellent way in which he has put this bill through and also to get my hand in

again to be ready for another pipe line bill that is coming before this house. When that bill comes before us I assure you that you will be hearing several forty minute speeches, especially if there is no difference in the form in which it was presented to the other place.
Those of us who took part in the building up of Canada last year without the assistance of certain hon. members, particularly those from British Columbia-I hope they have all seen the error of their ways and will support this bill-are ready to take that course again. My colleague to my left is the only one on this side who did see the error of his ways in time. I want to say to the hon. member that I shall do everything to see that he gets his line through and I shall also do everything in my power to prevent the passage of another bill that provides for a pipe line going first to the United States.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the assurance that has been given by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) that the route followed by the pipe line to be built by the company covered by this bill will be an allCanadian route makes it clear that there will not be an extended debate on this bill as was the experience in connection with certain other pipe line bills in previous sessions. We are glad to have that assurance so far as this company is concerned, for the lack of that assurance was one objectionable feature to which we took exception in certain other cases.
Even at the risk of spoiling the unanimity with which hon. members have been expressing themselves as being ready to give complete approval to this bill I should like to point out there are some of us in this house who regret that the government is not going into the construction of pipe lines for the distribution of gas and oil on a public ownership basis. When I say "some of us" I am happy to include the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson). While he does not belong to this socialist group nevertheless he has taken the same position on former occasions.
Hon. members must realize that there are some things that are natural monopolies, which should not be in the hands of private corporations but rather in the hands of the people through their governments. The particular commodity to be transported by pipe lines, gas and oil, is the type of product that lends itself, in our view, more to a crown corporation than to private interests.
The hon. member for Vegreville said he hoped there would be other companies coming
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines into the field. That takes us back to the old story in the past when competing and paralleling railway lines were built at great cost to the country in materials and manpower. In the end the people of the country have had to pay for that duplication and paralleling of railway lines. It seems clear to us that this is a field into which the government should be entering, either directly or through its own transportation system, the Canadian National Railways.
It is not our intention to block the passing of this bill, but we do feel that the viewpoint I have indicated should be expressed before second reading is given.

Mr. Speaker, I rise simply to deal with one point very briefly. When the province of Alberta decides that it has gas available for this purpose and when this company receives the authority it is seeking I should like to know if it will be in a sufficiently strong position to construct the line? I am assuming that when the bill reaches the committee the committee will satisfy itself that those who are seeking to do this thing will be capable of carrying it out. We should not be placed in the position of having given a great privilege to people who can turn it to their advantage without having the intention or capacity of carrying it out. I raise that point and repeat that I assume that it will be gone into before the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) in welcoming to the penitents' bench the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore). This project seems to be a most admirable one as far as I understand and it should get the support of the house unless, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat has suggested, there are some things which would make it appear that the project will not be completed.
One reason why I like this idea of a pipe line running from Alberta to the central provinces' is that if and when the natural gas in Alberta gives out the pipe line could still be used to supply gas or liquefied fuels to be produced from the coal fields which exist in such vast quantities in Alberta. That would be one means of putting a permanent end to the rather poor position we have been in, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, in our dependence to a large extent for fuel supplies upon the United States. It seems to me that a pipe line of this sort should be useful as long as it lasts in supplying the fuel deficiencies of these provinces.

The government will contend that the subject matter of this bill is covered already by the Criminal Code. I claim that the acts I am trying to forbid are special, and that my bill goes much further in prohibiting subversive activities, as nowhere in the code is there any mention of totalitarian dictatorship. In other words, can the minister show me where in the code there is a section making it a criminal offence to try to establish a communistic regime or to participate in such subversive activities? The best proof of that is that the communist party has never been outlawed in the code whereas, according to section 1 of the bill, no one will be allowed to be an active communist. Moreover, it is surely not by taking away the Canadian citizenship of those few foreign-bom communists living in our country after they have been convicted of sedition that we will be able to suppress the communist party in Canada since they will continue to have a legal existence and to spread their propaganda just as any other political party does.
The minister may say in opposition to the bill that it is much better to leave the communist party at liberty until war is declared because, through their mixing with the spies,

the R.C.M.P. would be in a better position to surround and arrest them when war was declared. This seems to me a bit obvious because, according to the report of the R.C.M.P., there are about 15,000 members of the communist party in Canada. In the meantime they will intensify their propaganda and fanaticize their supporters greatly. We must remember that, if war is ever declared, it takes the action of only one or two men to constitute an act of sabotage. Moreover, I submit if the bill is adopted it will not prevent the R.C.M.P. from following their usual course of action.
Are we going to wait for acts of sabotage to be committed to take action under section 133 of the Criminal Code which would then permit the government to act by invoking the sedition that this article of the Criminal Code contemplates? As to the second section of the bill, it is true that section 209 of the Criminal Code makes it a criminal offence to post obscene publications, and that section 207 makes it an offence to print, publish or circulate obscene written matter; but this again is different from printing, publishing and circulating matter with a view to establishing a totalitarian dictatorship in Canada. I should also like the minister to tell me where the broadcasting of matter of the kind I have just mentioned is covered in the code. Furthermore, even if there were some similarity between the provisions of the bill and certain provisions of the Criminal Code-I am unable to find any-should the bill not be passed inasmuch as it would have the double effect of clarifying and strengthening any section of the Criminal Code having a similar purpose?
If the subject matter of the bill is already covered by the code, which I deny, why was it necessary at the beginning of the last war to pass orders in council outlawing the communist party and its affiliates, and forbidding the circulation of communist papers? I refer the minister to section 39C of the defence of Canada regulations, consolidation of 1940.
May I respectfully suggest to the government that any Canadian citizen, whether of Canadian or foreign birth, should be deprived of his political rights upon conviction by the courts of having committed, either in acts or words, treason or subversive activities against our country? As the law now stands, a man duly convicted of subversive activities by the courts may be a candidate in any federal, provincial or municipal election, and has the right to vote or hold a public office. At a time when we are asked to make enormous sacrifices to get rid of communists from the outside, it seems to me that we

should make an effort to get rid of the communists here at home, as I know you will readily admit that it is most ridiculous to allow the communist party to continue its propaganda in Canada, thus indoctrinating its followers to the point where later on they may commit acts of sabotage.
With respect to the financial set-up of the communist party, may I suggest to hon. members that they read an article in the issue of the Financial Post of the 24th of February entitled: "There's Big Money in Communist Business Network". More than $1 million yearly in subscriptions swells the communist party funds emanating either from their co-operatives, stores, insurance and professional business or directly from the Russian government to run their big propaganda and subversive mill. They have a paid staff of 200 organizers, and last year they sent 100 people to Europe and Moscow on various missions. Are you going to stand for that? Of course it is for hon. members of the house to decide.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if this bill should
become law it will make our national holiday, Dominion day, which has been celebrated in Canada for many generations, a moving holiday; and the same will be true of Victoria day. Unfortunately when this bill came up for second reading the other evening there was no debate whatever. I presume very few hon. members were in their seats at the time; certainly I was not here. In any event the bill did not receive the consideration it merits and I believe it should now be given further consideration by this house; this motion for third reading presents that opportunity.
I am more particularly concerned about Dominion day, July 1. If this bill becomes law Dominion day will be celebrated on July 1 only if that happens to be a Monday. If it should happen to fall on a Tuesday then the holiday will be on Monday, July 7. We shall also be celebrating Dominion day on July 4, the great United States national holiday, just as often as we will celebrate it on July 1. I submit that if this step is taken Dominion day will become merely another week end and will lose most of its significance as a national holiday. It is the only great national holiday Canadians have. Hon. members will recall that on two or perhaps three occasions one hon. member has tried to have the name changed from Dominion day to Canada day. He certainly believed it to be the great Canadian national holiday, and I am sure every member in the house realizes that such is the case.
It seems to me one of the great weaknesses of the Canadian people, perhaps our greatest weakness, is that we pay too little attention to our traditions, our history and those things that make one think of Canada. Here is a holiday the main purpose of which is to help the Canadian people think of their own nation. There are other examples of this weakness of Canadians. There is the matter of a national anthem. I well remember a day or two after the armistice in November, 1918, being with some other Canadians in the crowded town square of Mons. There was

to be a march past of troops of the first army, and while we were all waiting there, with this tremendous crowd around, we heard the music of "O Canada" played on the bells-I have forgotten whether they were the bells in the city hall or in the church. I recall vividly the thrill I felt when I heard that music. We found that the Belgian in charge of the bells had gone to a great deal of trouble to find the music so he could play "O Canada" as a tribute to the men of the Canadian corps.

Statutory Holidays
That was thirty-three years ago; yet in Vancouver today the position is that while we have the melody, no one knows what to sing. We have two versions there. Some clubs sing the Weir version and some the Buchan version. The result is that when "O Canada" is played most people sing "Tiddely-um-tum-tum" for they do not know what words to use. That is just an example. We have the melody; we should decide on the words and adopt them for our national anthem.
Another example is the Canadian flag. As yet we do not have a national flag. The red ensign has been flying on this building for several years because the practice was authorized by order in council. During two sessions of the last parliament a special committee of the Senate and House of Commons considered what Canada's flag should be. They had several thousand designs in the railway committee room; they went to a great deal of trouble, and at the end of the second session brought in a recommendation favouring a flag something like the red ensign but with a smaller union jack in the corner and a maple leaf surrounded by a white border in the fly. That recommendation was almost unanimous; I think only one or two members of the committee voted against it, but nothing was done. The report was never considered by the house and no flag was adopted, so today we find ourselves without a national flag.
Another example was the way we as a people looked upon naturalization. Until a few years ago there was absolutely no ceremony connected with our naturalization procedure. New Canadians were made citizens without any formality, without any welcome, without being required to have any knowledge of our history, our laws or our customs. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was one of the leaders in having that condition improved and today, certainly in my part of the country, the naturalization procedure is much better. New citizens are welcomed, and there is an entirely different feeling about the whole thing.
Canada incidentally has naturalized far more people than any other nation of the British commonwealth. I believe literally millions of people have acquired citizenship in this nation through naturalization, and we are still getting immigrants. Thousands of them are coming here every year, and we hope there will be thousands more. Surely these new Canadians will expect us to have a day that we treat as a national holiday, not just a week end when we can go away for a picnic. They come from countries that have national holidays. One of the finest ways to impress them with what Canada

means would be for this country to celebrate its national holiday, and celebrate it on the proper day. If this change is adopted we will be bringing uncertainty into our national holiday, and I think that is a very bad thing. This House of Commons should be leading in the direction of encouraging the Canadian people to celebrate their national holiday on July 1. A great deal of fault lies right here in Ottawa, with the members in this chamber and in the other house. We should be giving the people of Canada the lead in celebrating Dominion day on its proper date.

I shall make a short statement first, and then I shall give the members an opportunity for questions when we go into committee. The purpose of the bill on which this resolution is founded is to provide that benefits to the agricultural industry of the Farm Improvements Loan Act of 1944 may be extended for a further period of three years from March 1, 1951. The act which was passed, as its title indicates, in 1944 was proclaimed to be in force and effective as from March 1, 1945. It was to continue in effect for three years from that date.
Perhaps for the benefit of members who were not here at that time I should briefly indicate what was the intent and purpose of the act. I believe that is best described in the introductory paragraphs of the annual report for each year since that time. It reads:
The primary purpose of the act was to fill a gap in the credit system which has been developed in Canada to meet the needs of agriculture. That gap related chiefly to the provision of intermediate credit, and certain types of short term credit to farmers, for the improvement and development of farms and for the improvement of living conditions thereon. The act aims at assisting, particularly, the average farmer who in the past has frequently not been able to secure bank credit for these purposes. It aims, moreover, at providing credit in a form and under terms and conditions which are convenient and suited to the needs and conditions of the particular farm borrower.
Then the introduction of the act lists the types of loans which will be regarded as farm improvement loans. A farm improvement
742	HOUSE OF
Farm Improvement Loans loan means a loan, first, for the purchase of agricultural implements; second, the purchase of livestock; third, the purchase or installation of agricultural equipment or a farm electric system; fourth, the alteration or improvement of a farm electric system; fifth, the erection or construction of fencing or works for drainage on a farm; sixth, the construction, repair or alteration of, or making of additions to, any building or structure on a farm; and seventh, any work for the improvement or development of a farm designated in the regulations.
In 1947, when the first two years had expired, the scope of the act was somewhat enlarged by a provision to include poultry farming. The original act had just permitted loans on livestock and fur-bearing animals. In 1948, when the three years ran out, the act was prolonged by parliament for a further three years, leading to the 28th of February, 1951, tomorrow.	At the same time land
security was authorized in certain instances. This latter step was considered desirable as enlarging the field of lending on the basis of such security.
By the terms of the original act, guaranteed farm improvement loans for the purpose which I read out from the act could be made by any of the chartered banks of Canada direct to the farmers. The government is made the guarantor of such loans to the extent of 10 per cent of the total amount of the loans made by any one of those banks. In the first period of the act, that is, from the 1st of March, 1945, until the 29th of February, 1948, the total liability of the government was limited to the total loans not to exceed $250 million. In that period, however, the total loans made amount to roughly $35 million. In the next three years the total liability of the government was to cover only the remainder of that $250 million, namely, roughly $215 million.

Perhaps I should briefly mention the only important changes in these regulations since the bill was last before the house. These changes were published in the Canada Gazette on January 24, 1951-last month. As the house knows, the government has taken steps to curtail all types of credit, as an antiinflationary measure at the present time. There have been restrictions of consumer credit and housing loans, and the chartered banks are now restricting business loans. A similar policy has been effected with respect to the credit provisions in this act.
The time for repayment of loans for the purchase of a motor truck has been set at a maximum of three years. Before, such loans could go over the whole period of ten years depending on the amount. The amount of loans for the purchase, and installation, and alteration and improvement of agricultural equipment and farm electrical systems has been reduced from 75 per cent to 66J per cent. In other words, instead of asking for one-quarter in cash we now ask for one-third in cash. For the construction, repair and alteration of farm buildings, instead of making a loan of 90 per cent we are now authorizing a loan of 80 per cent.
There have been no changes with respect to loans for the purchase of agricultural implements. As I pointed out 85 per cent of these loans have been for the purchase of agricultural implements.
The regulations also suggest to the banks the period for which loans of various amounts should be given. This, too, has been reduced somewhat. In loans up to $400 it is now suggested that they should have a maximum of eighteen months; in loans up to $750, two years and six months; up to $1,500, four years; up to $2,500, six years and up to $3,000, seven years.

In conclusion I wish to say that the Minister of Finance is most gratified by the growing confidence of our farmers in the usefulness of this act. This has been shown by the increase in the amount of loans each year. Farmers' associations across the country have been most helpful and have co-operated in every way, as have the banks.
There is just one other point I should like to make in closing this statement. The minister pointed out this afternoon, when the house gave permission to have the resolution presented at this time, that the present act expires tomorrow night. Because of the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, and the time taken by private members' days, it was not possible to introduce the bill any earlier this session. I am not asking this concession for myself, because in the House of Commons I have neither asked, given nor expected favours. Nor at this time is the government pressing this suggestion.
