speechtext: Has the government given consideration to another piece of legislation to accomplish that end?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Perhaps that question should be directed to the Minister of Agriculture or his parliamentary assistant because, as my hon. friend knows, my knowledge of agriculture is not very extensive. What I have here is the detail in connection with the operation of these particular loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to express my support for this resolution and to thank the parliamentary assistant for the comprehensive outline he has made respecting the operations of the act. Indeed, he has answered many things I intended to ask. He comes from British Columbia and understands the conditions in that province.
In British Columbia we have a great deal of timber land that must be cleared. Nowadays it is possible for a farmer to have clearing done under contract by the government, which has clearing equipment, and to arrange for payment in some cases over a period of years.
In some cases however that is not convenient. Has consideration been given to permitting loans for terms under this act, so that a farmer who wishes to borrow money for three years to pay off a contract to clear land is enabled to do so and thus earn the amount of the loan inside the three years from the land cleared?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I am grateful to Hansard, because through Hansard of three years ago I was able to anticipate that this question would be asked, and others as well. Three

years ago the hon. member raised the same point. Since that time the regulations for the improvement of land have been interpreted to include clearing. In last year's report on the operations of farm loans there were 5,359 loans made for a total amount of over $2 million for the clearing of new land, to the extent of 266,902 acres. So that the loans are being made for that purpose; and especially in those provinces where local governments have made available land clearing equipment, those loans have gone ahead.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I noticed the parliamentary assistant said it was proposed to authorize a total of $200 million beginning from now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
And it is
considered, having regard to the growth of loans over the last few years, that that will take care of the next three years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That is the estimate at the present time. Last year, as I said, there were loans of $63 million. With the restrictions in credit now provided in the regulations, and in view of the experience of the past six years, when we used $170 million, it was thought that a total of $200 million for the next three years would be a reasonable estimate of the needs of the farmers in this regard.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Has it been found that the alteration made three years ago with regard to the amount of security which may be taken has solved the problem which had made itself felt then, so that in effect loans are not prevented from being made because of technical difficulties?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That is quite true, especially with the longer term loans. It might not be so for the short loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Will the regulations under this act permit the making of loans for the rehabilitation of orchards in British Columbia which were wiped out in the winter of 1949-50? Would that be classified as an improvement? Is there any way in which loans for that purpose could be obtained under this act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
The amendment which I mentioned for the planting and purchase of trees had that in mind, but we must draw the line between a measure of rehabilitation and a business loan made to a farmer on the business understanding that he will be able to repay it. With that in mind loans may be made for both the cost of purchase and the cost of planting trees. But again it will be in the judgment of the lending institution to 80709-48
Farm Improvement Loans decide whether the farmer is in position to meet the semi-annual or annual payments.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Is there any way in which the government exercises a directive function toward the lending institutions? Can you exert some sort of pressure on them so that it could be used for that purpose?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: There is no pressure whatsoever exercised by the government, either in connection with this type of loan or any similar type of loan which is handled by the same administration, such as the veterans business loan. Qualified as our civil service are, they have not had the day to day business experience of the risks and business values which the bank managers of this country have. Our interest in this does not go beyond the extent of providing the ten per cent guarantee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: What is the average term of loans made in the past?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That was one question which I asked the administration, and also if they could break down the categories of loans. Unfortunately the records are not kept in that way, but we can give a good approximation. As I pointed out, the average figure for the loans is about $1,000. Eighty-five per cent of the loans are for the purchase of agricultural implements and those loans are limited to three years. Using a rough rule of thumb, the average loan is for $1,000 and is for less than three years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Did I understand the parliamentary assistant to say that the total claims against the government to date were $19,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: When a claim is made against the government does the government assume the responsibility for collecting the money? What is the policy of the government in so far as this $19,000 is concerned? Is a certain amount of it considered to be a dead loss? Has the government seized the machinery that would have been bought with these loans?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: The actual practice is that the bank itself, as it would do with any other business loan, makes every effort to recover what it can through usual legal means. It is only when the bank has exhausted every opportunity open to them that they make a claim on the government, which is investigated by our administration. Then the claim is on the books of our administration and we try to recover. There has been only $506 so recovered over two years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
When a bank has not been able to get its money and makes

Farm Improvement Loans a claim on the government, does it then disappear from the scene so far as that loan is concerned?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That is quite right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
And the
government then takes steps itself? While I am on my feet I should like to ask one more question. In the 1949 report it states that the banks have continued to give excellent cooperation in promoting the objectives of this legislation, both by way of publicity and generally to make the provisions of the act known. I am interested in the extent of publicity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: There are two ways in which they do it. First is through the ordinary, daily contacts between the bank manager and tie farmer who may come in, perhaps looking for a business loan. The bank manager may advise him how he can better get this particular kind of loan. The second is by means of one or two short pamphlets which were distributed to the farmers and which set out what he could expect under this legislation. The most valuable publicity is through the banks themselves in their daily contacts with the farmers who are endeavor ring to obtain loans.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I do not wish to delay this bill in any way and I should like to commend the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance for the splendid account he has given of the administration of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I do not know of anything that has helped the young farmers across Canada more than this act, especially since 1945. It has put the farm implement business on a cash basis, which arose out of the farm implement inquiry of 1937.
There is just one other thing I should like to say, a matter which was touched upon by the hon. member for Brant. Some effort must be made or some method devised to assist young farmers to start farming. I do not think there ever was a time in the history of Canada when farmers got more of the breaks to which they are entitled, but it is most difficult for a young man to start farming today. He may be a good worker and have a good reputation, but it is quite often difficult for him to get the first $1,000 or $1,500 with which to make a down payment on a farm. Once he has made that down payment he can get a mortgage or perhaps obtain assistance from the bank under this legislation. But he finds it most difficult to get started.
I know this government is sympathetic toward the needs of the farmers but they should devise some plan, to be worked through the chartered banks if necessary, to
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

help young farmers get a start in farming. After all, farming is still the basic industry of this country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I agree with the remarks of
the hon. member who has just spoken. It is true that it is almost impossible for a young farmer to start farming in 1951 unless he is able to obtain some capital, perhaps from his father or through a bank, mortgage company or in some other way. Unless the government comes to the assistance of young farmers they are not going to be able to start farming under present-day conditions.
I support the second reading of this bill tonight as I think this legislation has been of real benefit to agriculture throughout Canada. There is one practice that has been growing up that I should like to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. He may be aware of it. I asked the Minister of Finance about this last fall and he said he would have the matter looked into, but I did not receive a reply during that session.
As I understand the provisions of the act, a bank is allowed to take security in the way of a mortgage if the loan is for more than $2,000 and the term is greater than five years. I can tell the parliamentary assistant that there has been growing up a practice in my community, and I know this applies also to other municipalities, whereby the banks ask the farmers to deposit their titles before they are given loans under this act. I know of cases where the loan has been for a period of less than five years and for a sum of less than $2,000. If we want the young farmer to be able to start farming, in my opinion a bank should not ask him for the title to the small piece of land he may own. In my opinion the bank is then asking for a longterm security on an intermediate term loan. Therefore I would ask the parliamentary assistant whether he knows of this practice, and if something cannot be done to curtail it at least to some extent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I do not know of the practice but on Thursday when we are in committee on the second reading of the bill I will have a statement ready on that point.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Is there any provision in the act to assist young farmers to buy land?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Has this act any relation to the farm loan board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
The field covered by the farm loan board is a very different area from this. This measure is for the improvement of existing farms, the improvement and extension of the equipment on the farm, the house, the barns and that sort of thing. On the

other hand, the farm loan act is a different act providing for actual help in the purchase and acquisition of land. This act is confined entirely to the improvement of existing farms.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Has the farm loan board agents throughout the different provinces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: The Canadian farm loan board of course has agents across the country. The Canadian farm improvement loan administration has not. There is a total staff of just sixteen which handles the administration of the government's interest in these loans and also veterans' business and professional loans. These latter are the same type of thing but most of the actual work in connection with the processing of these loans is done of course by the chartered banks of Canada. The Canadian farm loan board on the other hand is in a different category because it does the actual lending and the inspection of the type of assets on which the loan is requested.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I may be all wrong but I was under the impression the farm loan board was almost out of existence, that it was not promoting any more loans, that they were busy trying to collect and were refusing to take any more. Is that right or wrong?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will be quite frank. As I said, I am not an agricultural expert. I have done considerable work on the bill but the only knowledge I have of the Canadian farm loan board is knowledge I have gleaned from their annual reports and from talking to the commissioners. I do know that the Canadian farm loan board is still in operation. It still has field offices across the country. It is still in the business of making loans. It of course is in active competition with other lending institutions, which is not the case with the measure involved before us.
In that connection I have one set of figures which perhaps I should have drawn to the attention of the committee. My mind was called to them by the comments of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture. They have to do with the question of financing agricultural implements. In the days before this act was introduced I am told that the common minimum rate of finance of agricultural implements was around 8 per cent. That is the effective rate because most of the rates specified were annual rates on the total unpaid balance which of course is only half the effective rate. The rate on the financing of trucks certainly went from 15 per cent to 18 per cent. As a consequence of the growing use of this legislation, we have had a tremendous change in the picture right across the country so far as the rates for instalment purchase of agricultural implements and farm trucks is concerned.
Farm Improvement Loans
From the figures available it now appears that 45-9 per cent of all farm tractors, 64-1 per cent of all combines and 50-7 per cent of all threshers purchased in Canada last year was with assistance under this act. When you take into consideration the considerable number of these articles that are undoubtedly purchased for cash you will see the great change in purchasing habits and how little use is made of other finance plans. So far as trucks are concerned, unfortunately it is very difficult to segregate farm trucks from other trucks, but I would expect that the same percentage would probably be true, that the purchase of around 50 per cent or 60 per cent of farm trucks is financed under the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I am very much interested in this measure. I noticed that the hon. member for Assiniboia tonight made a remark similar to that which he made some time last year. It had to do with farm improvement loans and was to the effect that the borrower was required to deposit the title of his property with the banker when he was granted a farm improvement loan. During the last four or five years I have done quite a lot of business with farmers through farm improvement loans, and I was very much interested in what the hon. member had to say. Therefore during the time I was home I made it my business to inquire of my banker just what the procedure was. It seemed to me it was rather unreasonable that a farmer should be required to deposit his title with the banker. The banker said to me that that was the case but it was only done in order to protect the bank from the borrower borrowing twice on his own property. If we look at it in that light I think we will see that the banks were right in doing that.
I am very much interested in the bill referred to in the resolution. I heartily endorse it. It is a great help to farmers in carrying on their business. At the present time I believe the amount that can be borrowed is limited to $3,000. I understand that figure was set in 1944. Since that time there has been a considerable increase in the price of farm implements. For instance, take a self-propelled combine. It would sell for $3,700 or $3,800 at that time, and now the same machine runs around $5,000. I wonder if consideration might be given to increasing the amount permitted to be borrowed through such loans. I understand that the losses under the farm improvement loans have been very small and in fact insignificant. The proposal has my wholehearted support at this time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I wish to speak as emphatically as I possibly can in support of the

Farm Improvement Loans remarks by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture a few moments ago. One thing I just do not quite see though is how he got the idea that a young fellow could start to farm with between $1,000 and $1,500. It seems to me he was exceedingly modest. I was talking to a successful farmer in my constituency before I left to come here, and he told me that it cost him in the neighbourhood of $16,000 to set up his son on a farm. The fact is that in the west it is necessary to buy very much larger tracts of land and it is generally necessary to have very much more machinery with the result that costs are completely prohibitive to the ordinary young man desiring to enter the farming business. I believe that the parliamentary assistant was exceedingly moderate. I suggest to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance that something will have to be done before long to help boys to get away from too large income taxes when they are trying to get established. I think also that the interest rate on these loans is too high. When you can get money from the Bank of Canada at two per cent it sounds absurd to be charging five per cent to the boys out on the farms who produce your bread and butter. It just does not go together to make sense, Mr. Chairman. If ever there was a time in our history when we needed production and should take every possible step to increase it, this is that time. So I commend this matter to the parliamentary assistant with the utmost earnestness, and ask him to do everything possible to see to it that adequate loans are made available on reasonable terms to good young men who want to go into farming. There is no sense giving a boy a loan he cannot possibly service with what he can make, so we will have to bring down the rate of interest and increase the period of the loan.
I should like to commend what was said by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture, and to express approval of this act. The people of my constituency were grateful to the government for bringing it in, and I am sure this latest change will be heartily welcomed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Prince Albert raised a point the government might well consider; that is, increasing the amount of money that may be made available. Today many farm implements cost between $4,000 and $5,000 each, and the limit available under this legislation is scarcely enough to make it possible to buy those implements.
The hon. member for Middlesex West brought up the possibility of making available some form of credit to young farmers trying to become established on the land. I suggest
[Mr. Blackmore.l

to the hon. member that he bring that matter to the attention of the government to see whether at this session we cannot have some amendment of the regulations of the farm loan board which would enable that board to make larger loans than they make at the present time. One hon. gentleman asks if the board is still active. It is very active and is making a large number of loans, but the maximum amount of any loan is fixed at $5,000 plus, I believe, $2,000 on a second mortgage. Today that is not sufficient to establish the average young man in agriculture. The price of land has gone up; the prices of equipment have gone up; the unit of land the young man must have in order to operate efficiently is much larger today than it was when the farm loan board legislation was passed. I believe the government would be well advised at this session to make a study of that act to see if we cannot have some amendment which would perhaps double the amount of loan that might be made. I think this is absolutely necessary, and I know it would be very much appreciated.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I should like to express appreciation of this legislation and the help it has been since it was brought into force in 1944. Certainly it has been of great assistance to many people, but on the other hand I believe we have rather outgrown the limit of $3,000. As the hon. member for Prince Albert said, when this legislation was enacted in 1944 we discussed it at length and in detail. At that time you could purchase a self-propelled combine for a good deal less than $3,000. Today that machine costs from $4,500 to $5,000. I remember that in 1947, two or three years after this legislation was brought in, you could purchase a diesel tractor for about $2,500. Today that tractor out where I live costs around $4,200. You cannot purchase any of the better types of equipment today for less than $3,000, though you could buy a great many articles of equipment for less than that amount when this legislation was brought down.
For quite a few years now the question of how many capable young men can get started farming for themselves has given us great concern. I do not know much about the setup in the east, but really I could not follow the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture when he mentioned a figure of $1,000 or $1,500. That would not get one a good piece of equipment anywhere in our country. I think something must be done, either by amending the farm loan board act or by bringing in a new act, so that a worthy young chap who wants to farm, who has the

training and background for it, can be financed and assisted. It is just about impossible for that young man to do so today in western Canada, and I believe in most parts of the country as well.
So while I want to express my appreciation of this legislation and the fact that it has been extended, I am sorry that those responsible have not seen fit to increase the maximum individual allotment by at least another $1,000, making it $4,000 instead of $3,000. However, I hope those in authority will try during this session of parliament to bring in some legislation under which a young man with the proper qualifications and background can be assisted to establish himself on the land. That would be well worth while and deserving of our best consideration at this time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I am quite in accord with the assistance afforded under this act to many young farmers. During this debate mention has been made of the need to deposit the title with the banker. Under this legislation is it absolutely necessary that a young farmer have a clear title to his property before he can get a loan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Perhaps this would be a good time to answer this series of questions. The first was raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert and others, suggesting that the present maximum loan of $3,000 might have been adequate in 1945 but is not now adequate. That matter was under review when the legislation was being drafted, but I would point out that the figures I had, and which I mentioned, showed that the average loan across the country, in almost every province other than Newfoundland, was in the vicinity of $1,000 or a little less, which would not indicate very much pressure on the $3,000 ceiling. When the bill is in committee after second reading next Thursday I will endeavour to be able to state just how many loans are for the full $3,000; but since the average across the country is $1,000, at the moment there would not seem to be much pressure on the ceiling.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Can you find out if any applications have been refused because they were for more than $3,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Even if a man applied for $4,000, and the bank said it could only give him $3,000, that would still show up as a $3,000 loan in the records.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: But I wondered whether there was any evidence of people trying to get more and getting none.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
That would be fairly difficult to ascertain from the records.
Farm Improvement Loans

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: When the parliamentary assistant is getting the information as to the number of $3,000 loans, will he try to compare the number of loans of that amount with the total number of loans in the particular area?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Yes, that will be done. The other point I would mention in this connection is that we have actually given what might be called negative assistance. If you study the restrictions we have imposed upon credit here you will find that they are not quite as stiff as those we have imposed upon consumer credit. For example, under our consumer credit regulations automobiles have to be paid for in eighteen months, with a 20 per cent down payment. Under this act trucks can be paid for during a period of up to three years. That is a negative help, if you will; but here again, as was pointed out by the Minister of Finance, one of our chief anti-inflationary weapons at the present time is curtailing credit as much as possible, and encouraging payment in cash.
The next point was made by the hon. member for Lethbridge, that the interest rate seems excessive. This point was dealt with at some length in the 1944 debate, which I read with much interest. I have done my best to make a comparison of this interest rate with other interest rates. The first and most obvious comparison is that the interest rates farmers used to have to pay for loans to finance these purchases, as I pointed out, were a minimum of eight per cent for implements and as much as fifteen and eighteen per cent on trucks. These, of course, often had in addition all sorts of service charges. So far as the individual farmer is concerned, there certainly has been a great deal of improvement in the five per cent simple interest of this act.
The next thing, of course, which must be considered in so far as an interest rate is concerned, is the class of security and the cost of actually inspecting and servicing these loans. The member for Greenwood is certainly much more qualified to speak on this subject than I am. Certainly when you are making a great number of small loans for fairly short periods of time, where the actual goods or securities in question may be on outlying farms some distance from the place of doing business, there will be charges and costs which are not experienced in the ordinary business loan in a city. Today the ordinary business loan in the city is at around six per cent. It is true that the farm loan board is charging only four and a half per cent. The loans granted by this board are
750	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Farm Improvement Loans larger loans on better security, and they are loans for a longer term, some of them up to twenty-five years.
Another thing which is perhaps forgotten when we are talking about this rate of interest on loans is just how much successful business you have to do in a lending institution to make good capital losses. Tracing through the loss of one average loan of $1,000, the first obvious thing is that at five per cent you would need to have twenty times that business or $20,000 of loans outstanding so that your five per cent return from these successful loans would equal your capital loss on the one bad loan. However, the five per cent return to the bank is not profit. I believe the bank would be very lucky to have a net return of perhaps eight per cent on their transactions, so there would be twelve times that loan necessary to return them in profit the loan they have lost, which runs to $240,000. I believe that factor is very often overlooked when people talk in terms of interest rates.
The keenness with which farmers of this country have, in recent years, turned to this loan system at five per cent to my mind is a good indication that it is an acceptable rate of interest when compared to other rates they paid before, or other avenues that are now open to them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: It is better than eight per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Yes, and that is said in the proper accent of a fellow Scot.
The next point which strikes this treasury board conscience I seem to be developing in the last few years concerns this matter of how desirable it would be to have an expansion of this act so that the farm loan board could provide the necessary capital to start a young farmer on a farm. I believe we all agree it would certainly be socially desirable to give help in this direction. The government has done that for just one class of person in recent years, and that is the veterans. After all they were a special responsibility of all the people of Canada, and under both the Veterans Land Act and the veterans business and loan act, we have extended quite generous loans to start veterans on farms, in businesses, in professions. But I am afraid were we today to embark on a program of making advances to all young farmers to start farming, we would quickly have pressure from members, like myself for example, and other members who represent fishing ridings to have grants made to young fishermen. Then, the members from Toronto and Montreal would have an equally good case for young professional men, doctors and lawyers who were opening up offices and so on. As parliamentary assistant,

I do not think I can say much about what consideration the government can give to a program of that size.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: What about the politicians who are starting out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Sometimes they receive
encouragement, and sometimes they do not. I think those of us who are here today have received some encouragement from our electorate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I should like to point out that the young farmer can obtain a loan from the farm loan board. We are just asking that he be able to get sufficient to start business.

speechtext:
I quite appreciate most of the things the parliamentary assistant has said, and the way he has said them. He has shown a considerable amount of sympathy for the situation about which we are talking. I do not see why the government should not stand this matter of capital financing to the degree to which it is necessary to obtain the production this country needs. If Canada needs a greater production of fish in order to help fight inflation, and everyone seems to agree that the best way to fight inflation is by production, then what better possible use could be made of the nation's credit than by advancing aid to those who produce fish? Similarly, if those who are producing bread and butter need aid, then it should be advanced. I think the time has come for us to broaden out considerably along the lines the parliamentary assistant has very wisely begun to outline. After all, money is the creation of the state.
If we are looking at it from the point of view of the lending business for the banks, that is one thing. But if we are looking at it from the point of view of bread and butter production, that is another thing. The latter is the thing for which we are looking. The banker can take care of himself. That would be my general reaction, so I would have no fear whatever and would certainly support the parliamentary assistant if he were asking for capital aid for fishermen.
There is another thing, and that is the reference to the interest rate. Let us bear in mind that since those eight per cent rates were charged the price of money has gone down. During world war I loans were made at five per cent, but during world war II loans

were made at three per cent. Money v as not a bit easier to get in world war II than it was in world war I, but we have simply changed our ideas as to how much money was worth. We have gone further from the idea that money is a commodity, something you can create. That would be my general observation, and I am sure that the minister will view that with considerable interest.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I might say that I think this is a splendid act. I especially like the way the banks have been making loans to veterans, even though they settled under the Veterans Land Act. The situation was entirely different in 1919 and 1920. Any veteran who settled under the old soldier settlement board was not able to get a loan from the bank.
There is one point I should like to clear up. If a borrower is not able to meet his payment owing to conditions over which he has no control, such as crop failure or hail storm, the banks are allowed to carry that payment over. What will happen at the end of ten years if the borrower is unable to complete his payment for the ten years and the banker is willing to extend the payment over another year? Will the bank still be covered by the guarantee, or will it be lost?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member has mentioned that because it is one point I had noted when it was raised in 1945. So far as the extension of loans is concerned because of temporary difficulties on the part of the borrower, that is provided for in the regulations. So far 5,868 loans have been extended. There are two different types of extensions. First of all, there is the extension which the banks themselves authorize. For example, we shall say a borrower has bought a truck for which he intended to pay in two years. He finds he cannot meet his payments, but the regulations provide he has three years in which to pay. The bank can give him an extension of one year merely by notifying the administrative offices.
If, on the other hand, at the end of three years the borrower cannot complete his payment then the bank must refer the details to the administration here for them to approve of an extension of the statutory period, and that has been done. As to what the policy will be at the end of ten years, that time still will not be even within the scope of this act. That question can be more properly raised three years from now when the act is again before parliament. If the present practice with regard to shorter terms less than a ten-year period is an indication, then I will say that the government will go on as the hon. member has suggested.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I can understand, Mr. Chairman, how the position I have been taking might not be very acceptable to the minister. As do other hon. members, I realize that the Indians are here to look at this bill, and they are expecting to look at the bill tomorrow. I realize that tomorrow is private members' day, and in order to get the bill through so that the Indians could look at it, according to the rules of the house, it may be necessary for the government to ask permission of the house to suspend the rules tomorrow for a time long enough to get this bill through. But I have a feeling that the Indians will feel far more as though they had been taken into partnership in respect of this legislation if they are given the privilege of talking it over in detail before this

house advances the bill one stage toward becoming an act. If I were an Indian that is exactly the reaction I would have.
The Indians have always considered themselves to be partners with the white men. All the treaties they signed indicated that the white man looked upon them as partners; but since the Indians signed the treaties they have had an excessively difficult time asserting their right to be looked upon as partners. The white men choose to disregard their claim for partnership.
I believe that has been one of the major factors in the general discouragement of the Indians throughout the country over all the years. I think today is a pretty good time to change our ways and take the Indians actually into partnership and say to them just as the queen's representative used to say: "The Queen is your mother." Well, let us say that now and mean it, and let us do it. Let us talk the thing over.
The minister mentioned Andy Pauli and other men from British Columbia. I know these men. They are outstanding men. The men from Alberta are outstanding men, and I presume that the men from the other provinces are equally outstanding.
Mr. Chairman, if they had had the opportunities you and I have had they would sit in the House of Commons with as great dignity and effectiveness as the very finest members in the house. They would occupy governmental benches with just as great dignity and effectiveness.
Why not allow them to participate in a free and open discussion of the bill which is to decide their fate for probably thirty years? That is the way I feel about it. I believe that if we just do not proceed with the bill tonight we would be wise. If the minister would say, "Well, I will do that for these Indians", he would never have cause to regret it, and I do not believe the House of Commons would ever regret it.
It might take us another day or two, but if we can give the Indians throughout the country the feeling that we honestly intend to be fair with them, it would be a wonderful step forward in making out of these men and their decendants the great citizens we all know they are capable of becoming, and we all desire they shall be. That is my general approach to the matter.
I should like to see this done: I should like to see the minister go to meet the Indians- as, indeed, he has already done; and all honour to him for his having done it. I think it is the first time a minister in Canada has ever done that. It has had a profound effect upon the Indians. I know, because I have talked with them.

If the minister would go to them tomorrow and. say to them frankly, "I want your advice on this whole matter. We are going to do this thing in partnership. If there are things in the act that you want but which we feel we cannot give you, we want to tell you frankly about them. We do not want to trick you into anything. If you cannot see it our way, just let us keep talking it over until you can, even if we have to defer the passage of our act for another year,"-if the minister would say that to them, I know it would' be helpful.
We are entering trying times. Thousands of these men may be called upon to have their sons don the colours of the nation. Well, we might as well have them feel that they are blood brothers, that they are really Canadians. A few days extra will not make any difference. If the minister were to say to them, "Now, look, if you people will just say so, we will make arrangements to have the house put the bill through first and second readings tomorrow", then, so far as I am concerned, 1 will do everything within my power to expedite that very achievement.
Then they would know that they had a hand in the passage of the bill. We could put the bill through so that they could see it tomorrow night, tomorrow afternoon, or perhaps the next day. And, even if they have to stay over in Ottawa an extra day, the cost of keeping them in the Chateau Laurier would not be very great-especially in times like these, when we allow such liberal expense allowances to our government representatives, even to the extent of $25 a day and the like. In those circumstances why not make a little bit of an allowance to some of these delegates, some of these great Indian people throughout Canada?
That is my general reaction to the matter. I would rather see us not put this resolution through tonight, and for the reasons I have advanced.
Then, I should like to say one or two other things which I did not have time to say this afternoon. These are facts which I am sure many hon. members would wish to have before them, as will also those thousands of people throughout the country who are vitally interested in the Indians and who will be happy to know that we are taking time to consider them.
This afternoon I referred to certain requests from the Caughnawaga reservation. I should now like to refer to certain requests made by the Alberta Indian association, because I think it is worth while putting these things before the house. The Indian association of Alberta is under the able direction of John Laurie, a school teacher in
Indian Act
Calgary who has worked so hard for the Indians in the last twelve or fifteen years that he is in danger of death from heart failure. This man has toiled inconceivably in order to have this brief prepared. He has called the Indians together and talked with them.
Here are the recommendations of those Indians, in convention. They say, concerning the act:
The provisions of the bill fail to provide for the logical second step in the progress of the treaty Indian, gradual extension of self-government and administration of reserve affairs. The bill admits the existence of only two grades of Indians-the incapable old-fashioned Indian who in mind and mode of life has made no real progress since the coming of the white man, and the Indian whom your government, in spite of all agreements and treaties of any kind at any time, proposes to catapult into the responsibilities of full citizenship.
It will be noticed that the wording there is moderate. The condemnation of the act is emphatic, incisive and definite. And it is very serious. Then:
2.	The provisions of the bill fail to provide for the continued recognition of the Indian as an Indian. That is his right by every moral precept. He does not wish to be a white man. He wishes to preserve his identity as an Indian within the protection of his reserve.
One more condemnation of the act!
3.	The provisions of the bill fail to provide that band membership must remain undisturbed as at April 1, 1950, and that the descendants of the present members must be guaranteed full privileges of Indian status within treaty or agreement.
4.	The provisions of the bill fail to provide that in all matters affecting the integrity of the reserves the administration and expenditure of all Indian moneys, whether revenue or capital, the consent of the majority of the electors of the band must first be had and obtained.
5.	The provisions of the bill fail to provide that hunting, fishing and trapping rights must be restored to the Indian as at the time of the treaties or agreements.
6.	No form of voting in any white man's election must be forced upon the Indian without his consent. It appears that such provision is being considered by an amendment to the Elections Act.
7.	The provisions of the bill fail to recognize that in the words of Lieutenant Governor Alexander Laird, "it takes two to make the bargain."
And may I stop there to observe that that is the very thought I have been trying to express to the minister since I commenced speaking after supper. Let the act be a bargain in which two peoples participate. It should not be a bargain made by one of them and thrust upon the other.
8.	Above all, we respectfully urge that a clause be written into the bill granting any Indian the right to appeal to the supreme court of their respective provinces in case of a dispute over the exercise of the discretionary powers which may be vested in either the minister or the governor in council.
This eighth paragraph is not in their brief, but it is the closing paragraph of a letter

Indian Act
written by Mr. Laurie on September 7, accompanying the Alberta statement. The other seven points are directly from the Alberta Indian brief. I would feel relieved if the minister could take each one of these points and show that there is no valid basis for the conclusion reached. If the minister can satisfy me in that respect I shall say no more. I will hasten along the bill.
Hon. members must know that I have lived alongside Indians all my life. My father took up a homestead bordering the Blood Indian reservation, with just a road between. As a little boy I rode on that reserve. I know the Indians and their trials and tribulations. If we continue with the discussion of this legislation long enough I shall tell the house about the experience the Blood Indian tribe had in 1918 at the close of world war I. This experience is set forth ably by a man who was the agent of the Blood Indians from 1898 on for some time. It is an experience that I believe every hon. member of this house would revolt at.
It involved the required surrender of large sections of their splendid reservation regardless of the needs of their children in the future. If every hon. member of this house heard the details of that whole arrangement which spread over four years and more and which was carried out by a certain Indian agent I know he would never lift a hand to forward this legislation until he had an unbreakable guarantee that never again in the future would any Indian agent or group of men be able to perpetrate on any group of Indians anything comparable with that experience. But it happened right in Canada on the Blood reserve.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Sounds like the maritime rights.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
It was a dreadful thing.
The worst thing about it was that no matter what the Indians thought about it, they simply could not get redress. I do not propose to go into that now, but it is a fact that I have had experience with things of that sort. I lived right there when that thing happened. I saw the lands that were attempted to be taken away from the Indians under what you might call compulsory consent. I have been over them time and time again,
I am in a peculiar position in respect to this matter. I am sure that if every hon. member were in a similar position he would feel responsible to do just exactly what I am doing and would urge moderation and great reservation in proceeding with this legislation. While it may not particularly 
interest the house, perhaps I might appropriately give some sort of idea of the position I occupy. In addition to being a member of parliament I possess as another set of credentials the fact that I was raised right close to the Blood reserve. I have ridden over that reserve ever since. I am a member of parliament for the Blood Indians and I am an honorary chief of the Blood Indians. It makes a difference when you are an honorary chief. You feel you have more responsibility.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: What is your Indian name?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I shall give it in good
time. I was initiated at the sun dance in 1945 by Head Chief Shot From Both Sides, Chief Cross Child and Chief John Cotton, and given the name of Motuskumau, "The Good Adviser." In addition to that I am director on the executive of what is known as the Kainai chieftainship, which is an organization comprised of thirty-five members who have thus far been selected by the Blood Indians as honorary chiefs from among their white brothers. This Kainai chieftainship organization was set up through the earnest efforts of Archdeacon S. H. Middleton in Lethbridge on December 14, 1950, with E. R. McFarland of Lethbridge as president. The aim of the organization is to help the Indians help their children to a better life.
I suppose that is enough to show the minister that some indulgence ought to be exercised on my behalf for appearing to be so uncooperative in the matter of advancing this bill. I want to be sure that everybody feels happy about it. Before I discontinue these remarks I should like to say that there seems to be considerable anxiety on the part of hon. members that the cost of giving the Indians the services they deserve is going to be so great, probably in the course of the next hundred years, that the nation will not be able to sustain it. A suspicion which prevails everywhere is that the Liberal government is endeavouring to "get out from under" the burden of supporting the Indians up to a standard of living they know the Indians should have, before the burden becomes too heavy. They are using their great majority in order to accomplish that objective and have been exerting a certain measure of pressure.
I am not saying that that is correct, but it looks as though it were the case. The changes in the act seem to be designed to enable men to limit membership on the reserve and to obtain greater control over things on the reserve.
There is no justification for the anxiety that we shall not be able to support the Indians. This nation has only begun its career of production and industrial and economic

development. As days go by we shall come more and more to see that where we can produce goods, we can produce money.
All we need to do is to devise means whereby the Indians can share in the production which we can so abundantly bring into being and which they will gladly help us to bring into being. All we need to do is to bring ourselves to the point where we can see that and then we shall have no anxiety about how many Indians there are. The only thing we shall wish is that there were more of them. I do not know of any Indians who are communistically inclined or even suspected, notwithstanding the way we have treated them.
I believe I have pretty well cleared away the reasons why we should not be urgent about passing this resolution. I am now going to ask the minister to explain away each of these charges that have been made. It is only fair that he have a chance to do that after all that has been said. If he can clear away these charges it may change my attitude in regard to the matter of letting the resolution pass.
I am going to give them to him one by one. First I ask him to show that the bill which he proposes to introduce does not fail to provide for the logical second step in the progress of treaty Indians, the gradual extension of self-government and the administration of reserve affairs. Will the minister state whether or not he considers that charge invalid?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants to see the bill he should permit this resolution to pass. He will then see that that provision has been made. In fact it was made by Bill No. 267. Bill No. 267 gave ample authority for every kind of self-government from the least unto the greatest, to complete citizenship. This objection to the bill was unfounded with respect to 267 and is equally unfounded with respect to the one that will be introduced after the resolution passes.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: The minister has answered very well but you know the words that he used are what we call weasel words out west. You can say everything that he said and justify it by simply saying: We are going to make all the Indians assume citizenship and vote, and the result is that by voting for members of parliament and M.L.A.'s they are going to become self-governing as we are. That is exactly what the Indians are afraid of, and everything the minister has said could be justified through that very interpretation.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I had that in mind to some extent but only to a very limited
Indian Act
extent. I was really referring to the powers of the band councils over the management of affairs and the moneys of the bands, which I think is what my hon. friend had in mind.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Ask him if they are still subject to veto.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: The question is: Can the decision of the band council be vetoed by the agent or the minister? If it can then obviously there is a power which overrules the band's decision and renders it of no avail. That has been the unhappy experience of bands in the past, and that is their fear today. What has the minister to say with respect to that matter?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the present Indian Act does not give band councils complete authority over the expenditure of their moneys, as my hon. friend knows. Bill 267 did not do that nor will the bill that is to be introduced do that for the simple reason that there are some things which must remain the responsibility of the government of Canada as long as they are handling the money of the Indian.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That is well answered. What other items are there, other than the handling of money, which enter into the ruling of a reservation? There must be several other things besides controlling their own money which enter into the ruling of a reservation. For example, there is membership in the band, and whether or not an Indian person shall be able to buy a portion of land, hold it himself, and probably in the course of a generation sell it to some person off the reserve. All such matters certainly come within the purview of band control or government over the reserve.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Have we disposed of No. 1 yet?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I am not sure that we have. I am trying to get all the details.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Because what my hon. friend is talking about now is a section later on which deals with the disposition of reserves without the consent of the majority of the electors of the band. I think he is referring to No. 4 which says that the provisions of the bill-that is Bill 267-fail to provide that in all matters affecting the integrity of the reserves, the administration and expenditure of all Indian moneys, whether revenue or capital, the consent of the majority of the electors of the band must first be had and obtained.
That is the only representation from any Indian organization asking for that amount of control over their own affairs. Most of

Indian Act
them feel that the council can deal with these things without having a vote of the majority of the electors of the band.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
That seems a rather satisfactory and straightforward answer. No. 2 is: The provisions of the bill fail to provide for the continued recognition of the Indian as an Indian. That is his right by every moral precept. He does not wish to be a ''white man"; he wishes to preserve his identity . . .
What would the minister say with respect to that?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
The present
Indian Act does not say anything about preserving the right of an Indian to be an Indian. We have never taken that away from him. No bill is taking it away from him. He may call himself an Indian forever.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: But the important question is, does it go further than calling himself an Indian? Can he enjoy and claim legally all rights which appertain to the status of being an Indian?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Now we will take No. 3.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: How many more are there?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
There are eight. I am sure everybody wants to know what they are, and I am sure that the minister wants an opportunity to answer them. He feels confident of being able to do so, and when he meets the Indians tomorrow he will be able to say* "This is what I said". No. 3 is:
The provisions of the bill fail to provide that band membership must remain undisturbed as at April 1, 1950 ...	....
Is this the case or is it not the case?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
It is not the case.
I cannot understand why the date April 1, 1950, has been chosen. It has no significance to me or the department. What the bill does do is define an Indian, and so far as I am informed those who are now properly called Indians will continue to be Indians under the new bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: But everything depends on what the meaning of "properly" is, how it is to be interpreted. That is where the trouble lies. Who is going to determine whether an Indian is properly a member of a band or whether he is not? Where does the jurisdiction lie? Does it lie in the band council, in the band membership as a whole, in the two together, in the agent or in the minister?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: It lies in parliament to determine the definition of an Indian. If my hon. friend is not satisfied with the definition of an Indian in the bill when he sees it he may move an amendment.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: The Indians feel that it does not properly reside in parliament. May I express the Indian's point of view? He says: We Indians made a treaty with the white people. We were equals with the white people. Why should a parliament consisting entirely of white men, towards the election of hardly any one of whom we contributed by a single vote, have the authority to determine the definition of an Indian? As far as I can see there is no answer. Here is one of their key points. I think I have said enough on that. The minister says the word "properly" is the whole thing.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I used that word because there may be people today who are not Indians but who are calling themselves such, and I would not want to be understood as guaranteeing that they would continue a status which they took unto themselves and which is not proper.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
The trouble is that there are some Indians who are properly Indians, and who have been ejected from the Indian reserves. I have this information. I do not know whether the minister has it. It has to do with section 5 of Bill 267. This is another letter from John Laurie, the indefatigable servant of the Indians, a man whose devotion to the Indians I find it almost impossible to understand. You would ordinarily expect a man to do something with the hope of some ultimate achievement. John Laurie can have no advancement as a result of all the work he has done and is doing. He puts the matter this way:
In the case of Robert Walker, formerly No. 83 of Driftpile band, the officers of the Indian affairs branch (Mr. McCrlmmon) were satisfied to accept a statement from an aged Indian (late Chief Estachi-kon) who could not speak English, and through an interpreter who had already been discovered! practising fraud in connection with his own children who were the progeny of himself and a treaty woman. This man was Charlie Anderson, interpreter at the Driftpile reserve.
The Indians assert that this man, and especially his wife, are well known trouble makers but the field officers have consistently protected him and dismissed any protests. It is true that the late chief signed an affidavit, but it is unlikely that he knew what an affidavit was. Is it not possible that the interpreter, Charlie Anderson, was determined to make others suffer because he himself had been in trouble? In any event the late chief repudiated his affidavit when an Indian of his band talked to him about what he had done. (Correspondence on this must be on file in the branch, as we submitted it). But his repudiation passed without recognition and the word of Anderson was accepted. Was it because the branch officers were determined to gain their ends that a fraudist was allowed to determine the destiny of another man? The man Walker was already thirty-three or thirty-four years of age. How could anyone establish Walker's parentage at that late date?
In this case the Indian was ejected from the reserve, quite unprepared to compete

successfully in the society of the white men. He had no recourse whatever to any tribunal but had to accept the flat of certain members of the department. What conceivable control could that band exercise over the disposition of this man Walker, who they maintained was one of their own members?

speechtext:
I am not
familiar with this particular case. If my hon. friend will send me the details I will look into it and give him an explanation.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I knew the minister would say that. I have already paid the minister one compliment, because I greatly admire him and I do not mind saying so. My goodness, we get so few bouquets as we go through life that it does not hurt to get or give one once in a while. But the Indians want some stipulation in the act that will render it impossible or at least highly improbable that such a thing will ever be repeated in any band in Canada as long as the Indians live. If that Indian had been free to take his case to the supreme court of Alberta and the decision had gone against him he would have had to do as a white man does when he loses a decision. As it was, however, all the evidence it appears was in his favour, all the facts it seems were in his favour, but he was ejected from the reserve with all his descendants.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I think the hon. member knows that I spent a whole day with the president and secretary of the Indian association of Alberta discussing this brief. They made certain representations with respect to the subject now under discussion, and I suggest that when my hon. friend sees the bill he may find that they are satisfied on that point, at least in part if not wholly.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I would be inclined to accept what the minister says, but what bothers me is that once we see the bill it will have gone through first reading, and the government with its steamroller can put it through second reading in spite of anything that can be done by all the people of Canada. That is the risk we run, and that is why I am very much concerned. However, the minister has given his answer; now let us take No. 5.
5.	The provisions of the bill fail to provide that hunting, fishing and trapping rights must be restored to the Indian as at the time of the treaties or agreements.
In that connection I am going to make this statement. I have never had the consent of the Indians to do so, but I am going to make it no matter how they feel about it. It must be recognized that a province has jurisdiction over the game and fish in that province. It must be recognized that a province must make regulations in order to protect and
Indian Act
preserve that game; and this applies to every province in Canada including Alberta. The Indians, of course, feel unhappy because they are denied the privilege of catching fish during a certain season, or shooting game of all kinds throughout the season. The answer to that cannot possibly be put into any act of this parliament, and I would not expect the minister to try to do so since he would have no constitutional authority. However, I repeat what I indicated in my talk this afternoon. Where the Indians find it necessary to hunt and fish in order to live, and that privilege is denied them because of the growth of civilization-that is the way you have to put it; because of the onward progress of civilization-provision should be made to make up their loss.
This, of course, represents a tremendous advance beyond anything men have dreamed of, but some such advance has to be made. Take beef, for example. Indians hunt deer and other animals because they need meat. If they cannot get deer or other game, we could produce the beef and let them have it. There is no difficulty about it, if we can only discover the proper method of financing. Obviously there is a way of financing, so I say in this case I would not expect the minister to put any such provision in the act; but I would expect some provision for making up to the Indian the loss he suffers in this way, and that certainly can be done. My heart simply bleeds when I think of certain Indians in British Columbia who used to live on salmon and who now find their salmon supply entirely gone, with nothing done to remedy the situation. However, I will not ask the minister to answer that unless he chooses to do so.

speechtext:
Before I do
attempt a very brief answer may I respectfully point to the clock and express the hope that we can finish this before eleven o'clock? The question of hunting and fishing regulations in all provinces will probably come in for a good deal of discussion while this bill is in the process of going through the house. I appreciate what my hon. friend has said, though it does not precisely agree with this recommendation. I believe he is right; I do not think we could put in the bill anything along the lines of the suggestion here. It is a very large question and one on which we will need a lot of advice and good judgment when the bill is going through the house.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
One could hardly ask for anything more. I am sure the minister clearly recognizes that there is a problem which must be met. It cannot be met by the only means the Indians can think of, but it can be met

Indian Act
by a sufficiently liberal allowance to those Indians who find themselves in this difficult position.
I am still watching the clock; I do not know whether I will go beyond eleven o'clock or not. It will depend upon how the minister answers these questions. The next is:
No form of voting in any white man's election must be forced upon the Indian without his consent.
It appears that such a provision is being considered through an amendment to the elections act. Will the minister make a pronouncement on that?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I think my hon. friend could have done that himself. He is quite aware of the fact that the amendment of the Dominion Elections Act last year did not force the white man's vote upon the Indian. He may exercise the franchise if he wishes. If he does not wish he need not do so.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
The important thing
the Indians were thinking about was whether or not there would be an additional amendment of the elections act. The minister naturally will answer that he has no control over that act, but just the same he is a member of the government; when he speaks he speaks for the government, and the government must be bound by what he says. Would the minister express it as his solemn conviction that there is in the mind of the government no thought of doing any such thing as changing the elections act so as to jeopardize the position of the Indian with respect to his citizenship?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I think that is a little too much to ask a minister. All I can say is that the amendment of last year speaks for itself. I think it was well thought out and will be justified by the passage of time.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
The chief difficulty I find is that deep in their minds the Indians feel they cannot trust the white man in respect to this matter. They know that by devices of this kind they can be dispossessed and turned adrift without adequate preparation to compete in the economy of the white man, and they will not be able to do a thing about it. I suppose the government cannot go any farther, but it should make a declaration, as binding as a treaty with the Indians, that for at least thirty or forty years no such thing as that will be even contemplated. I should go a little further on this point, and I am watching the clock. It should be recognized that until the Indians have been educated and trained in all branches of education in which we train our own youth, no one should even remotely contemplate such a thing as jeopardizing the Indians' position on

the reserve. In so doing they would be committing a crime against the Indians, for which there could be no compensation. I suppose that is the best thing we can do, but it is a matter of our attitude as a nation.
There is one more matter. Do the provisions of the bill fail to recognize, that in the words of Lieutenant Governor Alexander Laird, "It takes two to make a bargain"? What is the minister's opinion on that?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That particular quotation had to do with treaties and the making of treaties. As my friend has already pointed out, we are not dealing with treaties in this particular legislation. There are occasional references to treaties, guaranteeing their continued existence in one respect or another. The Indian Act has been on the statute books of this country from 1869, and from the recital I gave this afternoon of the efforts which have been made to ascertain Indian opinion concerning this bill, we have gone just about as far as anyone can be expected to go. This afternoon I assured the house that if out of the conference we are going to have there are opinions to be brought to the attention of the house, or amendments to be made, I shall certainly draw them to the attention of the house.

Now, that is good. This
is the last point. Is there any reason why we should not put a stipulation in the bill which will give the Indian the right, either individually or through the band council, to appeal to the supreme court of his province in case he feels he has been treated unjustly?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
this afternoon the member for Kamloops pointed out that at the meeting he attended the Indians felt that the act might be divided into sections in which there would be a part applying to British Columbia, having in mind the fact that those Indians are not under treaty. I think the point is clear that this bill, and the Indian Act, must cover all the Indians in Canada. There will be sections in the act which do not relate to the Indians in one province but to those in another. Now, that is understandable. Similarly, there are sections in the act under which a decision must be made administratively by the minister, and upon which I think the house would agree no appeal is necessary or desirable, in the interests of the Indian and the administration of the act.
On the other hand, there are certain rights the Indian may have which, if passed upon by the minister, may properly be the subject of reference to some other body, be it a supreme court judge or a county court judge; that is

only a matter of detail and can be worked out. I do not think my hon. friend would expect that, in every case where a minister made a decision, there should be an appeal to a judge. For example, if refusal is given to a loan under the revolving fund, would my hon. friend expect an appeal to the supreme court of Alberta concerning why the minister refused that particular loan? I do not think so.

I am in a position in which it is difficult for me and my colleagues to make a decision. It would be easy for me to carry the debate over eleven o'clock, but whether or not that is in the best interests of the Indians, I do not know.
